speechtext: The MINISTER OF JUSTICE (Hon. Charles Fitzpatrick) moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 265) respecting the Revised Statutes of Canada.
What progress has been made with the revision of the statutes and is it expected that the revision will be so far completed as to enable the law to be enacted by parliament next session ?

I am not quite sure that it will have progressed that far, but very substantial progress has been made. Over forty statutes have been completely revised and thirty-seven adopted. I expect that in December, more than one-third will be completed. I am not sure that the revision will be completed for next session but it will be in the Interval between next session and the session after.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.	-
I would like to ask my right hon. friend whether or not the contract with the North Atlantic Transportation Company has been laid on the Table ?
Not yet. There has been no formal contract, but correspondence which we have assumed to amount to a contract will be placed on the Table perhaps to-morrow.
The right hon. gentleman promised to make an announcement with respect to further government measures.
I shall make it to-morrow.

I would ask my right hon. friend the Prime Minister whether or not he has taken any steps to verify the accuracy of the alleged interview with Mr. Aylesworth, one of the commissioners on the Alaska boundary question.
I have not the telegraphic report at hand, but it contains rather extraordinary observations with regard to his duties as com-Hon. Mr. FIELDING.	1
missioner and also with regard to his views on matters now the subject of political controversy in the United Kingdom. It seems to me rather unusual, and I decline to believe that Mr. Aylesworth could have used the language attributed to him ; but inasmuch as the interview has been cabled cross the Atlantic-I am not sure whether by the New Canada Press Association or not-and has been commented on throughout the country to a considerable extent, it seems to me desirable that the government should ascertain whether or not it is accurate, and if not, inform the public and the country.

The government have taken no steps to ascertain whether this alleged interview has taken place or not. We assume that this interview had not the character attributed to it. Mr. Aylesworth is a counsel of very great eminence, and I would hestitate to believe-and I think my hon. friend would have equal hesitation-that he would have expressed any opinion on a matter which is sub-judiee and in which he himself is one of the judges. The language attributed to him is very improbable and until I hear to the contrary and have some better ground for believing that Mr. Aylesworth has so expressed himself, I shall believe that this interview, like many others, was not an expression of the views of Mr. Aylesworth.

subtopic: ST. VINCENT DE PAUL PENITENTIARY-MANAGEMENT OF THE HOSPITAL.

speechtext:
Mr. LEMIEUX by Mr. Talbot-asked :
1.	Is the honourable the Minister of Justice aware that the grand jury summoned for the September criminal term of the Court of King's Bench, for the district of Montreal, made a report blaming the management of the St. Vincent de Paul Penitentiary for the manner in which the hospital of that institution is kept 1
2.	Is it true that the hospital of the St. Vincent de Paul Penitentiary is conducted in a manner that conflicts with every law of hygiene ?
3.	Has the inspector of the penitentiary made a special report to that effect ?
4.	What is the nature of that report ?

subtopic: ST. VINCENT DE PAUL PENITENTIARY-MANAGEMENT OF THE HOSPITAL.
speechtext:
1.	No, but the minister has read the report as published in the newspapers.
2.	No, quite the contrary. The hospital contains three wards. One isolated on the upper story for contagious diseases, one for ordinary patients, and one for convalescents to exercise in. All are well lighted, by large
428 J
windows during the day, and* by electric light at night. They are thoroughly ventilated, comfortably heated and scrupulously clean. There is not a trace of damp. The floors are of hardwood, the bedsteads of iron, white enamelled, with spring and fibre mattresses. None of the patients sleep on the floor, as stated in the report referred to.
3.	No.
4.	The hospital was renovated in 1900. That year the warden reported :
The old hospital, as improved, affords to-day the accommodation so much needed in the past by patients, and if they have not the conveniences accessible in the Kingston penitentiary, they have at least improvements which afford them the hygienic means necessary to the recovery of their health. The isolating hospital for contagious diseases has already rendered important services in preventing contagion. A convict has passed through the phases of typhoid fever of an adynamic type. The state of this patient has caused the physician great uneasiness, but, thanks to isolation, the contagion has not, so far, claimed any other victims. (Page 19, report of Minister of Jhstiee, 1900).
The surgeon reported :
At last our old hospital has been repaired and improved, and has been at the service of the sick since the middle of May. (Page 40, same report).
In 1901 the Inspector reported :
The hospital is inconveniently located, but has been improved by the addition of a ward that doubles its original capacity.

speechtext:
Before you leave the Chair, Mr. Speaker, I desire to call the attention of tjie government to a statement which I see in several of the morning papers with regard to the Alaska arbitration now proceeding in Great Britain. The item is as follows :
Toronto, Oot. 10.-The ' News ' special cable from London says : ' I am informed on what may be accepted as high authority that a majority of the Alaskan commission will shortly give judgment adverse to the Canadian contention. It is understood that Great Britain's representative on the commission, Lord Alver-stone, has privately intimated to diplomatic and colonial office officials that he is convinced that a stronger case is made out by the United States, and that he intends to give judgment accordingly. A majority of the commission will thus agree upon a verdict and the two Canadian commissioners will, if they register in the issue, be unable to affect the result.'
I have quoted from the Ottawa ' Morning Citizen,' but I have seen the same item in one or two other newspapers. I am sure that the House and the country will be very glad to learn if there is any information that the government can communicate to the House on the subject.

subtopic: S U P P L Y-5A L A S Iv A BOUNDARY COMMISSION-OPINION OP BRITISH COMMISSIONER.
speechtext: I think this so antecedently improbable and almost impossible, that it does not require tiie slightest consideration at the hands of the government or any member of this House. I cannot conceive it possible that a person in the position of Lord Alverston could have committed himself in advance to delivering judgment in any such way as is stated in this despatch.

Before the motion for Committee of Supply is carried, 1 would like to say that there is a matter to be brought up by my hon. friend from Peel (Mr. Blnin) on going into supply. But I understand that it is more convenient for the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Rt. Hon. Sir Richard Cartwright) to proceed with his estimates this morning. We have every disposition to meet the right hon. gentleman's convenience, with the understanding, of course, that the House will be moved into supply later on.
' The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE. I believe it will be agreeable to bring the matter up on going into Committee of Supply, at three o'clock.

Motion agreed to, and House went into Committee of Supply.
Mail subsidies and steamship subventions- additional to service between Great Britain and Canada, $25,000.

This is for the purpose of meeting any possible additional subsidy that may be required under our contract with the Allans. We pay by steamer, and the rates vary, therefore, it is not always possible to ascertain in advance exactly how much will be paid. Of late, I may say the service has considerably improved. The ' Tunisian ' and the ' Bavarian ' have been making, during the last three or four months, very fail-rates of speed from Rimouski to Moville and back.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE (Rt. Hon. Sir Richard Cartwright).

speechtext: What is their general rate of speed ?
The general rate of speed by the steamers I have referred to is about 14 knots ; the others about 124 knots.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: The contract seems to be on a sort of sliding scale. Is it according to the number of trips made ?

speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: According to this, I assume that the minister has not made provision for the maximum outlay ?

Heretofore there has been a sum which has been available for this service- about $25,000, under the head of service from St. John to Liverpool. That has been dropped. So, this is practically no increase, because, in the past we were able to use this $25,000 in addition to the $150,000 voted for this service.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext:
Are we correct in understanding that the vote heretofore given to vessels by St. John via. Newfoundland to the old country has been dropped ?
The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COM-'MERCE. No, there was no vote for exactly that service. There was another vote. That vote to which my hon. friend refers is a vote of $20,000, not from St. John's, if my memory serves me, but from Halifax to St. John's, Newfoundland, and thence to Liverpool. That vote remains. When that was originally granted there was no calling at St. John's. It remained for a considerable time, and was not nearly used, except for the purpose of supplementing the vote to the Allan service.

I suppose it is through not clearly understanding the circumstances that I do not comprehend the necessity of the additional $25,000. Is it occasioned by putting on another boat, or is it occasioned by the fact that the sum paid to the Messrs. Allan is on a sliding scale ?

Yes, on a sliding scale, dependent on the speed and quality of the boat. Two of their boats receive a much better sum than the other. The ' Bavarian ' and the ' Tunisian ' are paid very much more than the inferior vessels employed. But of late they have been employing better vessels. The close of the South African war released a number of those craft, and we are now getting a better service.
Additional for steam service between St. John, N.B., and Glasgow, during winter of 1903-4, $7,500.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext:
Hon. gentlemen will observe that a similar sum is in the main estimates for the service heretofore run. We propose to
double that service, and give a corresponding sum, the total of which will be about $15,000. That service has been of considerable use in bringing us into communication with Glasgow and the population round about.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: How many vessels are they giving ?

We have a fortnightly service instead of a monthly service. They carry mails if any are tendered by the post office, but, of course, the mail service is not a very important portion. To all intents and purposes they are freight boats.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: Have they cold storage apparatus "!
They have summer accommodation. But the hon. gentleman will observe that this is a winter service. There is not much of a perishable nature carried by them during winter.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: What is the character of the freight, and is there any - return freight ?

It is of a very mixed character, all sorts of general cargo. They fill up with deals if they can get nothing else. They also carry large quantities of produce of various kinds. The return cargo is not large. It consists chiefly I am told of articles of iron and things of that kind. But the great difficulty we have to contend with, and the reason for giving more money in these subsidies, lies in the fact that the return cargo is generally very small. Still this service is of use in that it brings us into direct communication with a large and important centre of population in Scotland. In Glasgow and the surrounding district there is a population of a million and a quarter. It is a matter of considerable moment to us to have direct communication with these people for the purpose of facilitating the sale of Canadian products. I think the money has been pretty well spent.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext:
Do American exporters make use of these ships to send their produce in competition with our own ?
The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE!. That its chiefly in (Connection with the Canadian Pacific Railway. I am sorry to say they are not very much overburdened with cargoes. They take what they can get.

Is there any contract made with this company which prevents them from discriminating in freight rates ?
The MINISTER OB' TRADE AND COMMERCE. There is some regulation of that kind.
Is there any provision made by which the exporters of Chicago, for instance, shall not get better rates than those of Montreal, Toronto, Hamilton or any other points ?
There is a provision that they shall not discriminate against Canadian shippers.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: Can we see that provision before we adopt the item ? It is a matter of importance to the people of Canada, who are subsidizing these vessels, that greater facilities shall not be given American exporters by means of lower freight rates than are given to our own people.
I will send for the provision.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: I would like the item to stand until we get it.

I think the regulation should provide that not only should there be no discrimination, but that we should have a preference. What is the good of Canada paying out subsidies to steamship lines if we do not get any preference in rates ? If the Americans can come in here and compete with us in using these lines, what is the use of paying out Canadian money to subsidize these vessels to carry American freight ?
It is difficult to get a cargo as it is. It would not help Canadian freighters if you prevented discrimination.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: I am talking about giving a preference. If we give a large subvention, why should we not have a preference ?
It is not a large subvention, it is an extremely small subsidy.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext:
I think it would be better to give even a larger subsidy and to get a discrimination in favour of our own exporters.
Item allowed to stand.
Additional for steam communication during the season of 1903, between the mainland and the Magdalen Islands, $6,000.

This is a provision to double the accommodation heretofore afforded to these islands. The service for a long time was run weekly, and we paid $9,000 for it. They are now running semi-weekly, and they receive this additional remuneration. The boats are the ' Amelia ' and the ' Lunenburg.'
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: What are the mainland ports ?
Pictou and Souris.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: Are we doing much trade with the Magdalen Islands ?
A fair amount. Of course, with a double service we may expect to do more trade.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: What is the nature of the imports and exports ?

The Magdalen Islands belong to us. They send their fish down, and whatever is required for the use of the Magdalen population goes to them by this route. They have no other means of communication whatever.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: It is only fair that assistance should be given to the islands.
What is the population of the island ?

About 7,000 altogether.
Steam communication between Prince Edward Island, Cape Breton and Newfoimdland, $8,000.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: This is for the purpose of encouraging communication from Sydney to Prince Edward Island and incidentally to Newfoundland. I may observe that this vote* which is for $8,000 is granted partly in consideration of the reduction of the subsidy voted for a service between Prince Edward Island and Great Britain. We were giving them 810,000 but it was found very difficult to get a sufficient number of steamers. The vote has been reduced to $5,000 and in lieu of that we are proposing a service between Sydney and Prince Edward Island. That will be practically $3,000 of an increase on the two votes.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: From what points in Prince Edward Island will this service be maintained ?
Between Charlottetown and Sydney.
How frequent a service is proposed between these two ports ?
Our intention is to have a weekly service when the new contract is made.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: Has the steamer been selected ?
No, we have not been able to conclude our arrangements until we got the money.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: Would it not be possible to include Summerside in this arrangement ? The steamers that will perform this service will likely belong to some lines running between Montreal and Newfoundland. They pass Summerside and why not include Summerside ?

I shall be very pleased to do so if I can obtain the service. This, the hon. gentleman (Mr. Hackett) will observe is a new vote and we have not as yet been able to come to close quarters on the subject as to the number of places to be called at, but I will be very glad to include Summerside if I can possibly manage it.
Additional for steam service during the season of 1903 between Sydney, C.B., and Bay St. Lawrence and way ports, $500.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: This service is being a little enlarged. We have a service at present and we now propose to run it as far as St. Anne's bay. The steamer is the ' Weymouth.'
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: How do you come to put that item in here ? When does your financial year end ?
It is for the season. They have been giving the service on the understanding that we will put in the item.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: It should be in the supplementary estimates for the year ending 1903.
No, it is for the season and the season will not end until December.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: How frequent will this service be ?
This is a weekly service.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: Where is Bay St. Lawrence ?

It is in Victoria county.
Steam .service between Canada and Australia, $194,666.66.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: Is there any provision made in this contract that as a condition of our giving this subsidy there shall be no discrimination in rates in favour of American exporters as to the goods which they send to Australia ?
Yes.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: Would it not be well to supply the committee with that provision or arrangement ?

I think I brought it down. This is a repetition of the former vote we passed in the supplementary estimates for 1903, and 1 think, if the hon. gentleman will refer back, he will see that information was given.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: The right hon. gentleman may be correct, but if there is a provision of that kind, it can easily be brought down.

Yes, there is no objection. This formerly was a statutory vote, but the statute
has expired and in place of making it statutory we are now putting it in the ordinary estimates.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: What will be the amount of our contribution ?
There was an addition made last year, partly paid by ourselves and partly paid by Australia and Fiji.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: How much of the addition are we contributing ?

speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: Do these boats carry the mail ?
Yes.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: Is there any arrangement for cold storage or for special freight storage V
There are arrangements for cold storage.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: In how many of the boats ?
I think in all. The boats are the ' Aorangi,' the ' Miowera,' aud the ' Moana.'
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: There are three vessels. How many trips do they make in the season ?

There are sailings once every four weeks. A pretty considerable trade is being developed with Australia and it is an increasing trade as far as our exports are concerned. The imports are not so large.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: Is the trade of any considerable importance or is it increasing ?
The total amount of our exports was $2,586,554 to Australia.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: And our imports ?
They are very small. They amount to some $200,000 or $300,000.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext:
I drew the attention of the minister some years ago to the fact, that while our Canadian commissioners in these countries are promoting the question of Canadian manufactures and products, they might devote some time to the question of getting imports from these countries for Canada. For instance, in the matter of hides, Australia is a large exporter, and I believe we could profitably import hides direct from our sister colony. We should, I think, have a monthly freight service established from eastern Canada -the ports of Montreal, Quebec, Halifax
136S0

and St. John-and I am satisfied that if we did so, millions of dollars worth of hides could be imported from these colonies rather tka-n from foreign countries which have antagonistic tariffs against us. These hides are now taken largely to Holland and are then distributed to England and to Canada. I understand that at the present time, the Canadian service goes monthly, and the American service monthly also from the Pacific coast to Australia.
The American service goes tri-monthly from San Francisco.

I am satisfied that a large and profitable trade could be developed between Canada and Australia, even if we had sailing vessels plying from eastern Canadian to Australian ports. At present our exports have to be shipped across the continent to Vancouver, and the rail rates for such a long haul are absolutely prohibitive. If we could send vessels around the Horn from our eastern ports to Australia, it would be a great benefit to both countries. Has the minister given that his consideration ?

I have; but I am afraid any subsidy it would be within our power to give, would hardly produce the results which the hon. gentleman desires. We are doing a very decent export trade with Australia, but our import trade is very small; only $152,000 last year.
speakername: The MINISTER OP TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: A profitable trade could be done in furniture, if we could ship it direct to Australia, but it is impossible to send it by rail to Vancouver.
The journey from eastern Canada to Australia is nearly half around the globe; about 12,000 miles.
speakername: The MINISTER OP TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: I am aware of that.
It would be a very long journey, and would require, 1 am afraid, a very steep subsidy.
speakername: The MINISTER OP TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: The distance from Australia to eastern Canada is not so great as from Australia and New Zealand to German ports, and yet I was able to give figures some time ago to show, that the rates from Sydney, Australia, to Hamburg, on hides were less than the rates on the same articles from Chicago to Bracebridge, or other ports in Ontario by rail. I should think that the rates from Australia to eastern Canada would be less than from Australia to German ports.
When the Australian commonwealth begins to find its feet a little more, they may join with us.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: Of course I do not expect it to come about in a miuute.
I would expect more assistance from them than they have been hitherto giving, because that trade which the hon. gentleman speaks of would be to their advantage as well as ours.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: Certainly.
I have directed the attention of our agents to this matter, and possibly something may come of it.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: The great drawback is that our export trade has t6 be sent across the continent to Vancouver for shipment, and the railway freights must necessarily prevent anything like a large trade being done. You have either to send by rail to Vancouver or ship to New York, and when you ship to New York you cannot compete with the American exporters. If we had monthly steamers from Montreal, Quebec, St. John or Halifax, as the case may be, our trade with the commonwealth would be immense. I know of one firm that is ready to take a shipment of 3,000 tons of paper right away if they could only get it shipped direct from Canada. Ordinary furniture could be exported in what is called ' knock-down ' shape to be painted and put together when it arrives in Australia. Carriages of different descriptions, window sashes and doors, and other Canadian manufactures would find a ready market in Australia, because the tariff on most of the articles which we could export to that country is only 15 per oent. This is a question which is worthy of all consideration. I should hope that the Australian government would supplement our grapts to steamers. I am happy to say that the condition of Australia is improving very rapidly at present. The recent rains there have been most beneficial, and the reports are that there will be very large and profitable crops in the commonwealth this year.
Is the minister aware of the policy of the United States in respect to subsidizing vessels to different ports ?
I do not think they grant any subsidies to the lines to Australia.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: What is their general policy with respect to subsidies.

That matter has been under consideration in congress a good deal, but I do not think they have as yet formulated any policy. They have talked a good deal about granting subsidies, but unless it be to the Philippines, or some of their own possessions, I do not think they have granted them in the fashion we have granted them.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext:
Has the minister any information with respect to the trade between the United States and Australia ?
The MINISTER OB' TRADE AND COMMERCE. It is considerably larger than ours ; it is perhaps $8,000,000 or $10,000,000. My hon. friend from Toronto (Mr. Clarke) asked what were the provisions as to discrimination. The terms are as follows :
All passengers or freight that may be offered, or that can reasonably be procured, at rates which shall not be in excess of such maximum rates as are fixed by the minister, should it be advisable so to fix such maximum rates. And in no case shall any discrimination be made as regards rates, or otherwise, directly or indirectly, against Canadian merchants, or shippers who shall always have precedence for their freight and goods over all other merchants and shippers.
And It is agreed and understood that the freight rates on eastbound trips sailing from St. John. N.B., as hereinbefore provided on bills of lading through to Glasgow, Scotland, from any place in the province of Ontario, or Quebec or from any Canadian points further west, shall in no case be greater than from the same place to Glasgow via any United States route or port; and on west bound trips the rates from Glasgow to any point in Ontario or Quebec or other Canadian points further west, shall be as favourable as by any United States route or port to the same place.
If I apprehend the meaning of what the minister has read that makes provision that the rate collected from any point in Canada via this route shall not be greater than via New York or Boston.
Or any other United States port.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: What we are aiming at is to prevent discrimination as between Toronto or Hamilton or London or Stratford and Chicago or Detroit or any points west of these cities.
I do not think that can be met under this contract.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: Complaints have been made again and again that rates are given via Montreal, Quebec or St. John from Chicago-
By this line ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext:
By lines running from Montreal and St. John-that rates are given from Chicago to Liverpool that are much lower than the rates charged from Stratford, Hamilton, Toronto, or other great industrial exporting points in Canada, and there is no provision in this contract, if I apprehend the meaning of the words, to prevent such a condition of things. In the item which we are discussing, the steamship service to Australia, it is an indisputable fact, and the United States returns will establish it, that the exports of American products to Australia are increasing by leaps and bounds.
It would surely be bad policy on our part to give these enormous subsidies to establish a line of steamers from Vancouver to Australia if it is found that the owners of these ships make better rates for goods going from American points, Chicago and points in the eastern states, than are given to our exports from Quebec and Ontario ? We are actually paying a bonus to these companies to give an advantage to our competitors.
If my hon. friend (Mr. Clarke) will send me any detailed instance in which that has occurred, I will inquire into it at once.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: I think it is the duty of the right lion, gentleman to see that this is not done.
I do not know that anything of the kind has occurred.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: I believe it can he established.
Well, then establish it.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: I am not prepared to establish it at the present time, but I think that we should be sympathized with instead of being attacked for asking for information.
The hon. gentleman has a perfect right to ask for information.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext:
Is the right hon. minister, in asking this $200,000, prepared to say what the rates are from any New England point, say Boston or New York, as compared with those from Toronto or Montreal ?
The MINISTER OB' TRADE AND COMMERCE. I have not that information with me but I can get it.

Perhaps it would be well to let the item stand until the right hon. gentleman is prepared to give that information. I have heard again and again that goods from Boston are shipped at a lower rate via this route to Australia than goods .'from Montreal or Toronto.
If the hon. gentleman will produce any evidence on that point we will have the matter investigated at once.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: Surely if the right hon. gentleman is as jealous and zealous as he should be to guard the trade of Canada he should have all these particulars at his finger ends.
It is the business of parties who have complaints to make, to make them and to give their evidence. They have riot done so in this case.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: The right hon. gentleman admits that he lias no information on the matter and is not prepared to say what the freight rates are between these points ?
I did not say that.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: He made that admission a moment ago.

I have repeatedly in this House, even during this session, called attention to this matter and the right hon. gentleman promised across the floor of the House that he would look into it. I did not bring up the Australian case but I did bring up the fact that goods are shipped via Canadian steamboat lines to Liverpool at cheaper rates from western United States points than from the town in which I live and other Ontario points. The minister promised to look into these rates, to have them printed and laid before the House.
The hon. gentleman had nothing to say about the Australian rates.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: I brought up the rates to England from Canada and the fact that the American farmer, who lias never contributed one cent in bonuses to these railways and steamship lines, sends his freight by them to England and lands his grain there at a cost of five to ten cents a bushel less than what it costs the people of the county from which I come, who have taxed themselves hundreds of thousands of dollars to pay for these railway and steamship lines.

The agreement which the right hon. the Minister of Trade and Commerce has been good enough to place in my hand provides that the steamship line is to handle :
All passengers or freight that may be offered, or that can reasonably be procured, at rates which shall not be in excess of such maximum rates as are fixed by the minister should he deem it advisable so to fix such maximum rates ; and in no case shall any discrimination be made as regards rates, or otherwise, directly or indirectly, against Canadian merchants, or shippers who shall always have precedence for their freight and goods over all other merchants and shippers.
I would suggest that the difficulty raised by my hon. friend from Toronto (Mr. Clarke) would hardly be met by that clause, for it simply deals with discrimination against Canadian merchants or shippers and not with rates from points in Canada as distinguished from the United States.
Read a little further.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext:
Then the contract proceeds as follows :
And it is agreed and understood that freight rates on eastbound trips sailing from St. John, N.B., as hereinbefore provided on bills of lading through to Glasgow, Scotland, from any place in the province of Ontario, or Quebec or from Sir RICHARD CARTWRIGHT.
any Canadian points further west, shall in no case be greater than from the same place to Glasgow' via any United States route or port; and on west bound trips the rates from Glasgow to any point in Ontario or Quebec or other Canadian points further west, shall be as favourable as by any United States route or port to tbe same place.
The remaining portion of the clause relates altogether to cargoes of lumber or timber and prescribes the proportion which can be carried. So, it seems to me, that this portion of the clause will hardly cover what my hon. friend from Toronto (Mr. Clarke) has spoken of, because it merely provides that the rate from any place in Ontario or Quebec shall not be greater by this route than by a United States route. What my hon. friend from Toronto is dealing with is this. He alleges that he has been credibly informed that rates from Chicago or other United States points in the west via these lines are lower than from eorrespondingpoints in Ontario and the west via the same lines. That is quite different from anything specially provided for in the contract. Do I make myself clear ?
Quite clear.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: When the question of transportation was discussed whole pages of rates were presented to the House by hon. gentlemen who were familiar with the question. The hon. member for North Perth (Mr. Maclaren) gave the schedules of rates from his own district points, Stratford, and, I think, Listowel.

I rather misunderstood the point my hon. friend is taking. The point he is now taking, I understand, is that in fixing through-rates from Chicago the railway or steamship company might charge less than from Canadian points. He is aware that that is an excessively difficult question to deal with. He is also aware that these vessels, as a rule, go out of St. John scarcely ever with full cargoes. They are obliged to fill up with deals and other commodities of that kind. How far it would benefit us to interfere it is a very difficult question to answer.
speakername: Tile MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext:
I admit that, but I submit that tbe situation is a peculiar one, to say the least. The people of Ontario are willing that we should vote reasonable subsidies to assist tbe shipping trade in tbe maritime provinces, but we are being handi-caped in the matter of exports, if the allegations I have made are correct. If we desire to transport cattle, cheese or butter by these subsidized vessels, we have to pay greater freight rates from points in Ontario to Liverpool than are given to our competitors who reside in the United States and bill their products from Chicago. In the clause which the right hon. gentleman read to us, there is no provision to guard against

this discrimination. We not only pay a subsidy, but higher rates are charged our shippers than are charged our competitors in Chicago. The same condition applies with regard to exports from the New England states to Australia and the east. Lower rates are charged than our Canadian shippers have to pay. This should be remedied. If we subsidize these lines, Canadian exporters should not have to pay higher rates, but should be treated with at least equal consideration with those of the United States.

That is quite right. The point he makes is one worthy of serious consideration, but I would point this out to him as a business man. I-Iere we are endeavouring to build up tbis export trade from the maritime provinces. These people complain of the low subsidies given. They state with truth that a great deal of this trade from St. John is carried with a loss. If there was the slightest disposition to give a preference to American goods over ours, we have taken power in the contract to prevent that. But does the hon. gentleman think that we would benefit by prohibiting the shipping of American goods by that route and sending them to United States ports instead of St. John or Halifax ? We can easily prohibit the export of American stuff through our lines and over our railways, but I fail to see how that would benefit us.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: According to the hon. gentleman these ships do not take full cargoes, so that there is room in them for Canadian and other exports. It is an anomalous condition that we should subsidize steamers, and then find these steamers utilized by our American competitors at lower freight rates. That condition should not be continued.
What would you suggest ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: I would suggest a larger subsidy and prevent discrimination in rates, or cut off the subsidy.

That might be done, but the House would have to go to a far heavier expenditure than we are now making. Take a steamer 2,000 tons, and suppose she has 1,200 tons of cargo from Canadian shippers. If she has not more than the 1,200 she will be obliged to charge the Canadian exporter with heavier rates in proportion than if she were filled up from other quarters. And while you can compel American products to be sent by their own ports if you like, still, I am bound to say, nnless we undertake a very much larger expenditure than we have undertaken, and larger, I think, than my hon. friend contemplates or would approve, we shall find it very difficult to deal with that particular
question. He knows that the matter of the through-freight from competitive points- Chicago, for instance-is one of the greatest problems that are presented for consideration in connection with this whole transportation question. Now, if we desire that our people shall have the preference if they have stuff to sell, I am not clear, though the matter deserves consideration, that we can well help ourselves.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: If we have a steamer of 2,000 tons burden and only 1,200 tons of Canadian produce offers for her cargo, surely the people of Canada are paying the subsidy to have that 1,200 tons carried to market. If the vessel carries a full cargo what is the balance made up of ? It is made up of products which are to enter into competition in the common market with the Canadian products. And this American freight is sent to our ports only because the rate is lower than the rate by American ports. Surely this is an anomalous condition of things- that the people of Canada should pay, in the first place, a subsidy to a vessel to take our products across the Atlantic, and then pay a higher rate than those who have products to sell in competition with ours, and who are not called upon to pay any share of the subsidy.

Well, to continue the illustration of my hon. friend, how would the people of Canada benefit if we compel this 800 tons of American products to go by New York ? They would enter into competition with Canadian products just as much as they do now, and the shipmaster would be obliged to charge a higher rate on the Canadian products than he now charges. I do not deny that the position is awkward and anomalous. But I point out the very great difficulties in the way of solving the problem which the hon. gentleman speaks of unless by undertaking a very heavy expenditure, and, ill any case, preventing competition.
Mr. HUGHES (Victoria)* I think the Minister of Trade and Commerce has misunderstood the position of the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Clarke). The hon. member does not want to prohibit the carrying of American freight, but I think he desires that the freight rates on the American goods shall not be less than on the same class of goods sent from Canada. In other words, we should not bonus the steamer to take Canadian goods to foreign ports and then allow that steamer to call at American ports and take similar commodities at lower rates.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: None of these steamers call at American ports.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext:
It would be well for the minister, I think, to look into this matter of the freight rates. I believe there is a good deal in the contention that our sub-

sidized lines are carrying American products at lower rates tlian they give to Canadians. Of course, they say that when they take freight at Chicago to be carried through, they have to take it at what rates they can get, and that it does not hurt the Canadian shipper whatever those rates may he. But, at the same time, if they can carry American products at 20 cents per hundred pounds I do not see any reason -why they should carry Canadian products at 30 cents per 100 pounds for the same class of freight. I find also that subsidized lines running from Canadian to other ports are very loath to meet competition. I would instance the Bickford & Black lines from Halifax to the West Indies. They are obliged to meet competition from New York, but they do not meet it until the last protest is entered. They do meet it finally, but they are a long while about it, and as soon as an excuse offers, they raise the rates again. They may carry flour for the Americans for 20 cents a barrel and there is no reason why they shrfTdd not do the same for Canadians. If they receive a subsidy from this parliament, then, we sboud make it a condition that they shall carry Canadian produce at as low rates as those they give to the Americans. If the minister would inquire into this and see that such a condition is carried out, I believe it will be only fair and would be in the interest of Canadian trade. Bait I advise him that it takes a good deal of vigilance, to have such a condition carried into effect. They are very wary and you have to be constantly ascertaining what the freight rates are at Chicago and you have to be always on the alert.
The rate is made by rail and water. The steamships themselves do not carry freight for the round rate.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: They ' divvy up ' with the railways. There is an understanding between the railways and the steamship companies. This, would be a matter well worthy of the minister's careful consideration.

The discrimination in freight rates does not ncessarily affect the Canadian shipper in the market to which the goods are sent. Of course, if the American shipper undersells the Canadian by reason of the discrimination, then of course the discrimination is a matter that very injuriously affects the Canadian. But if that is not so, I do not see how the Canadian shipper is very much injured by reason of American freight going through the Canadian channels. On the other hand, it helps us to get the service of a less subsidy than we should get it for if American freights were not allowed.

I think my hon. friend (Mr. Fowler) has hit the exact difficulty of the situation. I have made inquiries and, so far as Mr. CAMPBELL.
I can learn, competition on the other side of the water is not affected by what goes through by these steamers. Everybody knows that the amount of American produce which goes to England is enormous ; and it is so enormous that the comparative trifle that goes by those lines does not affect the prices.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: There is another point that should not be lost sight of, and which goes to benefit our friends in the maritime provinces. There is, for instance, a rate from a western Canadian point to St. John. There is a through-rate from that western Canadian point to Liverpool. In that case, the through railway rate to St. John would be less than the direct railway rate to St. John. On reaching St. John, an arrangement is made with the agent of the steamship company by which, for some trifle, these goods are not taken across the water but are taken out and disposed of to the merchants of St. John and other places. In that way the merchant profits by the difference between the through-rate and the local rate to St. John, which amounts to something considerable. I understand that this practice is carried on to a very considerable extent not only in our Canadian seaports but in American seaports as well. I think the minister could make his department, if he intends remaining in it, one of the most beneficial in the whole service to the public, if he would take hold of these freight rates, both through-rates and rates in bond and make comparisons, and publish them to the shippers of the country.
I notice in the contract which wTas read that the minister has the right to make a maximum freight rate. Has he done so ?

As a rule these people have all been complaining that the route is not a profitable one, and that the rates they maintain are so low that they can hardly make the two ends meet. From inquiries I have made I think that for some time, until a trade is built up, it will hardly be advisable to exercise that power. I have made careful inquiry into the question. Hon. gentlemen will understand, without dwelling on the subject, which is one of some delicacy, that to attempt to build up our winter ports has its difficulties. They are at a longer distance from the Canadian centres of production than the American ports, and we must make some considerable concessions in order to draw trade of that nature. Take the case of goods going from Montreal. If they go to Portland, it is scarcely 300 miles ; if they go to St. John by the Canadian Pacific Railway, it is 500 miles ; if they go from Halifax I think it is about 750 miies by the shortest possible route from Montreal. These are geological difficulties, and can be palliated by legislation but cannot be removed. Up to the present time I think there has been a gratifying increase in trade from

the maritime provinces, particularly from St. John. Still, trade has to be conducted under a good many difficulties, some of which we hope to remove. Some of those difficulties are discrimination in the matter of insurance, which is higher than it ought to be. Still we cannot shut our eyes to the fact that we are working to some extent, I must say, against natural obstacles, and therefore we have not attempted to cut down the rates that they can obtain.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: It seems to me that if it be found that less rates are charged to American shippers than to Canadian shippers the government would be justified in making a maximum rate above which they should not charge Canadian shippers, because we pay a portion of the cost of running those lines, whereas the Americans pay no portion.

I make bold to say that if the right hon. gentleman will instruct the officers of his department to make inquiry as lo through-rates from the New England states, and the through-rates from Chicago to Liverpool and Glasgow, he will find that the statements made here are fully borne out by his officers. If that is found to be the case, I think it deserves the serious attention of the right hon. gentleman and that he should see that such discrimination no longer continues against Canadian shippers.
That will be a matter for the House seriously to consider. But absolutely to refuse American goods coming to our various jjorts is a thing I would hesitate to recommend to the House.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: I point out the anomaly, that we continue to pay these subsidies when they are practically used against us.
It is quite true that from such points as Chicago, where there is a vigorous competition for European trade, the anomaly does exist.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext:
The question is not without difficulties, some of which have been pointed out by the right hon. gentleman. But I should hardly think they point to the necessity of a prohibition of the vessels from carrying American goods at those rates. The position of the right hon. gentleman seems to be this, that if you fix rates from Chicago equal to those which are paid from corresponding Canadian points, the result would be that having strong competition from Chicago, you would not get the cargo which is now procured. That would seem to be the position of the right hon. gentleman. No doubt many coinplicated matters have to be considered, to some of which he lias alluded, that is to say, that if you do not take this freight which is offered from Chicago you increase the cost, it may be argued, to Canadian
shippers, because you take that much away from the net earnings of the vessels crossing the Atlantic. However that may be, it certainly does seem an anomaly that while the Canadian government is paying a certain subsidy to these steamships-in this case it happens to be about $15,000 a year, but the same principle would apply to cases where the subsidy is much greater-it does seem to me an anomaly at least, whether it can be corrected to the advantage of the country or not, that Canadian shippers should pay on that line subsidized by their own money a higher rate of freight than that which is paid from corresponding points in the United States. I think my right hon. friend recognizes that as an anomaly. .
I admit it, but my hon. friend will also recognize the difficulties that I have pointed out. You are between Scylla and Charybdis, very often, in matters of this kind.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: Something like it is presented in the transportation problem which has been investigated by the United States Railway Commissioners. This subject has also evidently been under the consideration of this government in drafting the Railway Commission Bill which we had this year, because it is obvious that certain provisions in that Bill contemplated circumstances of this kind. I think the right hon. gentleman should take the representations of my hon. friend from Toronto (Mr. Clarke) into careful consideration, and ascertain whether it is possible to remove this great anomaly, one which must be considered a grievance by Canadian shippers, because they naturally feel that there is no reason why they should pay higher rates on these lines subsidized by their own money than are paid by United States exporters.

That is quite true, and the matter deserves consideration. But my hon. friend has incidentally struck on the real difficulty, which besets, both the Interstate Commission in the United States, and which will beset our own commissioners when they come to deal with the question of deciding what is to be done with the rates charged from competitive points. You see at Chicago you are within 800 miles of the ocean via New York, and a little longer to Boston, and not much longer to Baltimore. You are at the same time, if I recollect right, at a distance of 1,250 miles to St. John. I am not quite certain of the distance, but it is several hundred miles longer to St. John ; and if you turn away the freight which you can get from that quarter, you produce results which I have pointed out to my hon. friend from Toronto-we will have to pay a much larger subsidy if we deprive ourselves of the chance of getting a certain amount of freight from competitive points.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: Coming back now to item 95-steam service between Canada and Australia-is that subsidy practically payable to tbe Canadian Pacific Railway Company ?
It is a separate company which, runs these vessels. The New Zealand Steamship Company is subsidized by the New Zealand government and by the Fiji government as well as by ourselves.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: It seems to be a new item.
Tbe reason is that heretofore it has been in the statute, but the statute expired last year, and we have not renewed the statutory provision.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: You are making an increase of ?50,000.
Yes.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: Why ? Are you getting any improvement in the service ?
We are getting a little better service, but the fact is that we could not have the service performed for the amount formerly given. The parties refused to perform the service for the old subsidy.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: What is the improvement in the service which justifies the addition of $50,000 to the subsidy ?

They are giving us a better class of vessels than formerly, but the chief reason is that they distinctly declined to go on with the service for the old subsidy. We had either to pay more or to drop the whole thing. As the trade is increasing very largely, I did not feel justified in refusing, particularly as the Australian government, who are in favour of maintaining amicable relations, strongly advised us to pay a little more, and intimated their willingness to pay more.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: What portion did the Australian government pay before and what do they pay now?

speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: What does Fiji pay ?

speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: Is that a new subsidy to the line ?
No, they always paid a little.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext:
Is their contribution increased ?
Sir RICHARD CARTWRIGHT, i
There is a trifling' increase.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: Does New Zealand pay anything ?
New Zealand was paying something, but we dropped that subsidy, because the New Zealand service added a very considerable length of time to the trips.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: Are the boats not calling at New Zealand ports ?
Not at present.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: Why not ?
Because they were not willing to pay the subsidy.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: If they were getting no advantage out of it, I do not see why they should pay, but if we were getting any benefit out of it we should have the boats call at New ZealamJ ports.
Calling at New Zealand ports added considerably to the length of the trip.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: I have had the privilege of travelling over the route two or three times, I know all about the distance, and I know that it would not take very much time to call at New Zealand ports. Do boats call at Brisbane ?
Yes.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: I venture to say that the extra distance would not be so great that it would add very much to the length of the trip. A very large trade can be worked up with New Zealand. New Zealand is going to be in the near future the British island of the southern hemisphere and I would be very sorry if any action were taken on the part of this government, even if the New Zealand government do not see their way clear to contributing towards this subsidy, which would result in taking these steamers off the New Zealand line.
It would take a couple of days to go to New Zealand, and that is a matter of considerable importance.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: How is it that this subsidy is not payable to the Canadian Pacific Railway ?
Because they do not own tbe boats.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: I see here in their statement the ' Empress of India, the * Empress of China,' &c., for the service of which steamers they receive a subsidy.
That is the Japan subsidy. That is under the statute. It has nothing to do with this service.

Every four weeks.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: Two of the three vessels named by the right lion, minister have been performing that service for years. There has only been one vessel put on.
Yes, it was simply because they refused to perform this service unless we increased the subsidy that we have made this addition.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: We had to increase the subsidy or the service would be dropped- is that the situation ?
Yes.

Mr. BORDEN Halifax). Of an efficient character ?

Hon, Mr. HAGGART. speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: We have heretofore been paying $2,000 for this service, but it has been represented to me very strongly for some years back that it cannot be done at that rate, and we have agreed to give $3,000 in the future.

speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: You are increasing the subsidy ?

speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

They are semi-weekly.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

Steam service between St. Catherine's bay and Tadousac during the winter of 1903-1904, $2,000.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: There is a good deal of settlement going on now along the north shore of the St. Lawrence, and heretofore they have had nothing but a canoe service.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: Where is St. Catherine's Bay ?
It is on the St. Lawrence, on the eastern entrance to the Saguenay river.
Is this an experimental vote ?
Yes.
What is the distance between St. Catherine's bay and Tadousac ?

The distance is not very great. Quite a number of new industries have been established and quite a number of complaints have been made as to the means of communication, and it is said that this ferry across the mouth of the Saguenay is indispensable.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: How many trips will be made ?
They will make as many trips as they can in a day. The distance is about a mile or a mile and a half.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: What county is St. Catherine's bay in ?

Chicoutimi and Saguenay. The people who are on the east side of the Saguenay, when going to Quebec, have to drive up on one shore to St. Alphonse, cross on the ice there, and come down the other shore when they are going to Quebec. It is hoped that this ferry will save about 70 miles of a journey. Messrs. Price Brothers have an important lumber industry at St. Catherine's bay, and they are willing to make the experiment this winter with their steamer, in consideration of this subsidy.
It would seem that this is a service which should be performed by the government. The ferries are not run by the Dominion government.
Ferry licenses are under the control of the federal government on navigable waters.

On the St. John river, the ferries are subsidized not by the Dominion government but by the local government. There is a ferry in my own constituency at Milledgeville and that is entirely kept up by the local government. It does seem to me that the province which the Minister of Justice represents, is singularly favoured inasmuch as these services are performed by the Dominion government in that province, which have to be performed by the provincial governments in other provinces. I quite understand how important it is to the people of this section to have this ferry; I have no fault to find with that, but it does seem to me that it is a service that should be performed by the provincial government of Quebec rather than by the federal government.
The MINISTER OB' JUSTICE. The question of the ferry at Quebec was under the consideration of our courts and it was decided-and no one has disputed it-that that service was strictly under the control of the federal government, and that we could give licenses for ferries to cross the St. Lawrence on the same principle that we give

authority to construct a bridge. Quite recently the question has come up in Ontario-
With regard to Sault Ste. Marie.
The provincial government issued a license, and it was found to be of no value,
That was un international matter, and there is no comparison.
I should certainly think that no ferry, such as this at St. Catherine's should have a subsidy.

The ferryman has as good a right as any one else to use navigable waters as a public highway, and the only question remaining is, who should assist him. The ferry from Halifax to Dartmouth, crossing navigable waters, is established altogether under provincial enactments. We have various ferries throughout our province, over navigable waters, and those that are assisted at all are assisted by the provincial government.
For services of the steamer ' Lord Strathcona ' and wrecking plant on the St. Lawrence for the year ending June 30, 1904, $10,000.

speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: Might I ask the right hon. minister, what steps are being taken to improve the situation ?

The Minister of Marine and Fisheries has. been exerting himself in that direction, in the way of better lighting, better telegraph communication and other things which I hope will have a beneficial effect.

Mr. Speaker, before you leave the Chair, I wish to move an amendment which reads as follows :
That all the words after ' that ' to the end of the question be left out and the following substituted therefor :-The expenditure in connection with the taking of the census for the year 1881 was $511,550 for a population of 4,324,810 ; that the expenditure in connection with the taking of the census for the year 1891 was $549,991.76 for a population of 4,833,239 ; that the expenditure in connection with the taking of the census for the year 1901 is $1,198,268.99 for a population of 5,371,315 and the accounts for the census year 1901 have not all been paid.
That in the opinion of this House the said expenditure for the year 1901 is excessive and extravagant.
You will notice by the figures contained in the resolution that the increase in the population, as shown by the census of 1901 over that of 1891, was 538,076 and the increase of the cost of taking the census for 1901 over that of 1891 was $648,277.23. You will observe by tlnese figures, Mr. Speaker, that it cost considerably more than twice as much to take the census in 1901 as in 1891. In looking over the debates of parliament I see that when the items for the payment of the accounts of the census of 188i were up for discussion the Reform party, who were in opposition at that time, strongly condemned the Liberal-Conservative government then in power because of what they called the extravagant expenditure. In 1891 when the census of that year was up before parliament for discussion the same thing occurred. Some hou. gentlemen who now occupy government positions were then sitting on this side of the House and they used very strong language in condemning the Conservative government for the extraordinary expenditure and the inaccuracy of the census taken in that year. On looking over that debate we would naturally expect that if the time should arrive when these gentle-Sir RICHARD CARTWRIGHT.
men should come into office, as they did in 1896, a new condition of things would prevail. We naturally expected that when they came into office some of the pledges they gave to the people of Canada in respect to economy of administration would certainly be put in operation. In so far as expenditure in taking the census of 1901 is concerned the manner in which the promises were fulfilled was very disappointing to the people of Canada and it is for that reason and some others, that I propose to move the resolution that I now place in your hands. "We would naturally expect. Mr. Speaker, that some advancement would be made by the Parliament of Canada during ten years of Canada's prosperity. We would naturally expect that this government in 1901 would be able to apply some new rules in advance of those adopted by the Liberal-Conservative government in 1891. As you know, a great many changes have taken place during these ten years and it would be expected that the Minister of Agriculture would he able to take advantage of some of the municipal advancement that has taken place in the different provinces and apply these rules to the taking of the census in 1901. I wish to give an illustration in this respect. In the county I have the honour to represent there is a township called Toronto township. It was assessed by the municipal corporation in 1901 at a cost of $135 which was paid by the municipal council. Two assessors were appointed for that municipality in the year 1901, and I wish to point out, Mr. Speaker, what the assessors' duties are in the province of Ontario-I am not so familiar with the other provinces-the instructions are very complete the assessor on entering a house enumerates everything that is there. Let me read for illustration some of the schedules in the assessors' roll for the municipalities in Ontario. In column 22 he takes down the number of cattle upon the farm ; in column 23, the number of sheep ; in column 24, the number of hogs ; in. column 25, the number of horses ; in column 26, the number of births.
I could go through a large number of columns put into the assessor's hands as he commences his duties in the spring of each year. If you look over the schedules placed in the hands of the enumerators, when the census was taken in 1901, yon would see a very large number ot' columns like those I have read. When I remember that in that very spring of the year 1901, the people in every municipality of Ontario were called upon to pay their assessors for taking down these items, I find it strange that the hou. Minister of Agriculture did not take advantage of their services, and thus cheapen the cost of taking the Dominion census. I would not venture so far as to say that a complete copy of the assessment rolls would be sufficient for the Dominion census ; but what I do say is that if every ten years the Dominion

government were to place the additional schedules in the hands of each of the assessors in Ontario, each assessor would be able to give the government a complete and accurate census of every municipality in that province for a great deal less money than was spient in 1901. 1 repeat that it cost the municipality $135 to assess the township I refer to in 1901. That assessment was done by two assessors ; but when the Minister of Agriculture went to take the census in that township he put on nine enumerators, where two did the work for the- municipality, and it cost this government, not $135, but $433.45. The increase in the number of enumerators was seven, and the increase in the cost was $298.45, and the popula lion in each was the same, 5,208. I. throw out the .suggestion for the benefii of whoever may fill the position of Minister of Agriculture when the time comes to take another census. I think that some of the assessor's work, in the province of On tario at least, should be utilized in the taking of our census. My hon. friend the. Minister of Agriculture made a statement, during the discussion of these census items last session, that a great many more ques tions were asked in 1901 than at the previous census. That may be true, but many of those questions were altogether unnecessary. There were questions that did not bring out any valuable information, and some very important questions were omitted. For instance, in the columns which the enumerators had placed in tlieii hands, there was no column for fallow land I asked the hon. minister why there was no such column, and he replied because there is not much fallow land in Canada. Surelj that must have been a reply made in haste, for if he is at all conversant with the agricultural interests in Ontario, if he knows anything of that interest in other parts ol: this country, he must know that there is a very large quantity of fallow land. You cannot travel through any part of the province of Ontario, but you will find that on almost every hundred acres there are from ten to fifteen acres of fallow land each year. Let me ask my hon. friends from Ontario, who belong to the legal profession, what they find when drawing up leases. They will say that there is generally a clause providing that the tenant, when the lease expires, must have ten or fifteen acres fallow land. Why is that put in ? Is it because there is no fallow land in Ontario ? No, but because there is a large quantity of fallow land in that province. 1 asked my hon. friend from Macdonald (Mr. Boyd) the other day what about fallow land in Manitoba and -the Territories. He said :	We fallow a great deal of land in
Manitoba and the Territories ; it would be difficult for us to seed it down, because we do not want hay, as we have more than we can use. and no market particularly for it.
429i
Therefore the only possible way by which we can clean our land from weeds is to leave it fallow. Any gentleman who has travelled through Manitoba and the Territories will see thousands of acres which are under fallow. Yet, notwithstanding that, my hon. friend the Minister of Agriculture tells us that the reason he put no column for fallow land in the census of 1901 was because there is very little fallow land in Canada. He may say that is not important, but to my mind it is. If it is important to put a schedule in the hands of the enumerators, showing the number of acres of wheat and oats, why is it not equally important that we should have a record of the number of acres in fallow ? If a gentleman who wished to engage in agricultural pursuits in Canada were to take up the census returns, and if he were an advanced agriculturist, he would ask whether the farmers of the Dominion were forgetting what is the best means of cleaning the soil of weeds, not finding any fallow land in the census columns, he would conclude that the Canadian agriculturist did not know his business. Everybody knows that it is important for the farmer who wants to keep his farm in good condition and clean from weeds to have some fallow land.
