So it will be seen that under t-lie Liberal-Conservative government, the wickedness of which, in always finding offices for its supporters, lion, gentlemen opposite are never tired of dwelling upon, offices to the number of 124 were filled in connection with the taking of the census of 1891 in these six counties. But under the preseut government, and in connection with the census of 1901, the offices were increased to 200, or 70 more than under the Liberal-Conservative government. I see my hon. friend from South Brant (Mr. Heyd) in his place. Let me give the figures with regard to his riding. In 1901 the cost of taking the census there was $2,683.52, the population being 26,707. In 1891 the expenditure was $1,488.78, and the population 23,357. It will be observed that in this case the population increased by 3,348 and the cost of taking the census by $1,194.74. I am one of those who believe and expect that the cost of taking the census in 1901 would be more than it was in 1891. But I do not quite understand that any of these central counties in tile province of Ontario-and the same applies to almost every county in Canada-where there are fewer people, it should cost so much more, in some cases nearly double, to take the census. I am a little suspicious that there has been some political influence at work. This is not always charged against my hon. friend the Minister of Agriculture, but I rather think that in this case he is guilty. In looking over the returns for the county of my hon. friend from East Peterborough (Mr. Lang), I notice some explanatory correspondence. We would naturally expect that a business government, proposing to take a census, would carefully prepare a statement of the enumerators' duties, have it put in the form of a circular and sent to all the parties interested ; and that, having made a careful arrangement as regards the duties of the [DOT] enumerators, they would be able to decide the basis on which those enumerators should be paid. But this is not the case in the county of my bon. friend. The commissioner in East Peterborough put in his account and payment was refused. Some vouchers were not forthcoming. They were not very particular about vouchers in many cases, i must say. There was some little difficulty about the items in East Peterborough, and my hon. friend (Mr. Lang) wrote some letters to the department. And
in the statement given by the department of the Minister of Agriculture the following memorandum appeared : ' Im view of the letter from Mr. Lang, a revision of the account has been made. The accountant has used liis discretion in allowing board items, and this might be explained to Mr. Lang in writing to him.' That looks like political influence, does it not ? The Minister of Agriculture says :	I discharge my duties
without regard to political parties. Yet, when an account comes into the hon. gentleman's department and the payment of it is refused, my hon. friend (Mr. Lang) writes on behalf of his supporter, and, as soon as the letter is received, the word goes, ' pay the account.' Why ? Because it was a just account ? Was that the reason ? If so, why was it not paid without my hon. friend's intervention ? The Department of Agriculture prepared the statement laying down the duties of the enumerators and giving full instructions, so that accounts might be put in correct. But my hon. friend interceded, all that w'as necessary was some political interference, and as soon as my hon. friend wrote a letter to the department it was all right, and the account was paid.
That was for board.

In looking over the items, X find one for over $2,000 for telegrams sent out to the enumerators. Why was it necessary, within a month after the instructions were given, to pay $2,000 for telegrams ? Was it because the minister bad taken pains to prepare and issue correct instructions ? No, it was because the instructions that were sent out were in some cases incorrect, and the minister had to telegraph all through the country to the commissioners in the different counties, at a cost to the people of Canada of over $2,000, in less than six weeks. But that was not all, for when these enumerators were called together they were in some cases kept from two and three and five days awaiting their instructions from the government under this hon. gentleman. Let me read a paragraph that will throw some light upon it. In the county of East Peterborough, John Kerr, was commissioner. In writing to the department about his account, he makes this statement over his own signature :
You will see that considerable expense has been incurred for which neither the enumerators or myself were responsible, on account of the necessary books and papers not being received on time.
Who would be responsible 'for that ? Surely that could not be blamed upon the hon. gentleman who represents the county, nor upon the enumerators or commissioners. These men were called together at central points from different parts of the county, and when they got there they were kept in the leading hotels at the cost to the country

because the papers had not been sent out on time. Another item in that letter says :
James Pengelby and Charles O'Reilly of Norwood should each be allowed six days. They -were both here for three days the first week. But as the papers had not been received and they had to return the next week for two days.
That is, they waited for three days for instructions after being called together. I wish to make the statement that in any opinion there has been some negligence-shall I say some political interference 1 I leave the House to judge on that point. Now, I wish to refer to the county of North Hastings. Mr. Kelly was commissioner for that county, and he had a very large bill, amounting to 5P653.14. He put in his bill, but there was some little dispute about it, and it was not paid at the moment. So Mr. Kelly says : * I will get after this government.' Of course lie understood what kind of ammunition was required to reach the minister, and he says : ' My plan would be to get a leading Reformer in my county.' And he sought out the nominee of the Reform party for the local legislature in that county, Mr. Lott, and Mr. Kelly and Mr. Lott came down to Ottawa after payment of the account had been refused, Mr. Speaker-these gentlemen came down, and Mr. Lott used his local political influence with the Minister of Agriculture. The two gentlemen came down together, and interviewed the minister. Here is Mr. Kelly's letter to the Minister of Agriculture, I will only read one paragraph :
When I met you in the House of Commons on Thursday last in company with Mr. Lott.
It is proved over this gentleman's own signature that he came down to Ottawa in company with the Reform nominee for the local legislature for that county, and they interviewed the Minister of Agriculture. With what result ? That is the important point. No one can complain of that gentleman coming down to interview the Minister of Agriculture, that of course would be part of his political duty ; but when the country has to pay for this interview, then the opposition have a right to complain. Now what was the result? Listen to the letter written after he went home to the Minister of Agriculture, dated at Marmora, 24th March, in which he says :
The Ontario elections are coming off the end of May or the beginning of June. Mr. B. 0. Lott is the unanimous choice of the Liberal convention. I have made up my .mind to do some hard work in this north riding of Hastings. Mr. Lott is the best canvasser and the hardest worker ever went into a political contest.
I have the honour to remain, your old servant,

He seems to have had a good deal of political familiarity with the hon. Minister *of Agriculture. Now what was the result of the interview ? As soon as the minister gets that letter from Mr. Kelly, the accouut is rectified, and a letter goes forward from
the department to pay him. When was it rectified ? is the question I would like to have answered. If the account was a correct one put in by Mr. Kelly for $653.14, the ,commissioner for the county, if that account was in accordance with the schedule of prices laid down by the minister in giving his instructions to the commissioner and the enumerators, then my hon. friend should have paid the account at once, there should have been no dispute, Mr. Kelly had a right to his money. But let the House take note-just as soon as they brought this political influence to bear, indeed, almost before that hon. gentleman reached his home, a letter went out from the department to pay the account and Mr. Kelly got his money.
The Minister of Agriculture threw up his hands.

Well, he threw up the purse of Canada for the amount I have mentioned. Now, Mr. Speaker, that is about all I have to say. I could go on and give many more instances, because X have made an extended investigation of the different counties. What I have to.say is. in the first fflace, that the people of Canada expected better things from the hon. gentleman.
They don't know him as well as we do.

Well, they will know him better soon, I suppose. The complaint we make is that when these hon. gentlemen were sitting on this side of the House in 1881 and 1891, they strongly denounced the Liberal-Conservative government for taking' the census at such an extravagant cost, and we are surprised now, as the people of Canada must be surprised, to find that after these economicial gentlemen get Into office and come to take the census, they pay for it double the price that the Conservative government paid, although there is but a small increase in the population. We complain that the census taken by this government, so far as the agricultural interests are concerned, is an incomplete census, and it does not come up to the requirements of the country. We make this charge moreover against the hon. gentleman, that in regard to some of these accounts at least, the hon. gentleman has weakened, and has yielded to political influence, and has done what otherwise he would not have done, and should not have done in the interests of the country. We charge that political influence has been exercised upon the department, I do not know how far it has been carried. But we have found some instances where political influence was brought to bear, and I suppose if we carried our investigations further we would find many other instances. We say that we condemn this government for this excessive expenditure. We say further that some more advanced methods should be adopted, that these hon.

gentlemen should have learned something during the ten years from 1891 to 1901, that they should have profited by the advanced methods that have been adopted by the different municipalities in Canada and that they should have applied them to the taking of the census. In this country the functions of government overlap. Assessors are employed in every municipality in the province of Ontario,, and they take the municipal census. This government came forward and they increase the number of men employed even in those counties where the papulation has decreased, but the time has come when the people expect the government shall make some advance in the matter of the taking of the census. I am not quite sure that the lion. Minister of Agriculture will occupy that position at the end of the next decennial period.
Oh, yes, he will.
The hon. member for West Huron (Mr. Holmes) says * yes he will.'
And he is quite correct.

I congratulate these hon. gentlemen upon their opinion. Well, we differ about that. I would like my hon. friend from Haldimand and Monck (Mr. Thompson) and my hon. friend from West Huron to go back to their counties and try to give an explanation to the electors how it is that this so-called economical government found it necessary to expend so much more money to take the census in 1901 than was expended in 1891.
We will be there.

If the hon. gentleman applies the test of municipal government to his county he will find that the methods of this government will meet with general condemnation from the electors. I would expect that hon. gentlemen opposite would vote for this resolution. It is a mild condemnation of the extravagance of the government in connection with the taking of the census in 1901 as compared with the cost of the taking of the census of 1891. I beg therefore. Mr. Speaker, to move the amendment which I have read.
