Roughly speaking, between 70 and 60 per cent. I may say that this schedule of rates was carefully considered before the work of taking the census was commenced. It was discussed with those who seemed to have knowledge in such matters and it was agreed upon as a fair rate to be paid for the work to be done. It was agreed upon without any reference as to how it would work out or as to what the totals might be when the census work in toto was paid for. It was established on the ground that a fair day's work should be got and a fair day's wages should be earned by the person doing the work for the country, and,
I may say here, at once, that to a large extent tlie increased cost of enumeration was due to the increase in the schedule of rates.
What proportion of the total cost does the cost of enumeration amount to 7

The enumeration of the census of 1901 up to the present time has cost $878,000. Had the rates of pay been the same in 1891 as the tariff in 1901, the census of 1891 would

have cost $767,000 making allowance for the increase of population or only $111,000, while the information obtained in 1901 through the 657 questions as compared with the 216 questions in 1891 is infinitely greater and well worth this $111,000 extra expense.
What about the other expenditures ?

That was in the schedule of rates, but in addition to that we found it was necessary to make an allowance for horse-hire and days of instruction. We paid for the days of instruction, which was entirely apart from the pay under the schedule rates, and which was exclusive of the time occupied in the direct taking of the census. The horse-hire was due almost entirely to the desire to have the census taken more rapidly, and the work put through so as to get the returns in with greater speed. That object was also aimed at by the rule that we should take a census enumerator for each polling sub-division instead of for a larger area. That of course involved a greater number of persons to be instructed, and consequent increased cost. The result was a much more rapid taking of the census and we believe it was worth some sacrifice to attain that end.
Is the work of the census completed yet ?

I am speaking now altogether of the enumeration, and that was completed long ago. We had also the fact that certain unorganized districts were enumerated in 1901, and were not taken into the count at all in 1891. That is not only the case with regard to the far off Yukon and the northern parts of our territory, but it also refers to districts in organized territories, and even in the old provinces of Ontario and Quebec, which were counted in 1901, but which in 1891 were simply estimated in the office here at Ottawa. In the census of 1901, the whole country, whether thickly or sparsely settled, was taken into the actual count, and the census of 1901 is a de jure count of the population of the Dominion, whereas the census of 1891, with respect to a large area of our Northwest Territories, a considerable area of partially organized territory, and a considerable area of the province of Ontario, was merely an estimate made in Ottawa, and was no census at all. This added materially to the cost of the enumeration in 1901.
How much ?

I cannot say exactly how much, but the hon. gentleman will understand that the taking of the census in the older portions of Canada was easy and inexpensive, compared with the counting of the population in these remote districts. The fishery enumeration in
1891 cost $2,245, and in 1901 it cost nearly $14,000. As a matter of fact the fishery enumeration in 1891 was so inefficient that the figures were thrown aside and no compilation made of them, whereas in 1901 the information is carefully compiled and will be valuable for future reference to the people of Canada.
Can the minister tell the difference between the cost of taking the census in Prince Edward Island in 1891 and in 1901 ? There are no remote or sparsely settled districts in that province ?

I have not the figures at hand with regard to Prince Edward Island, separately. In consequence of the desire to get earlier returns we had to employ a larger number of enumerators which involved, of course, greater expense.
What urgency was there for an earlier return than in the case of the previous census ?

The answer is obvious, that the sooner we *Can get these statistics the more valuable they are. If we are to drag along for nearly the whole time between the two censuses without getting these returns, they are of comparatively little value.
Were the returns available for the public use earlier than they were in the case of the previous census ?

Yes. If the hon. gentleman has patience I will give him that information. The enumeration was to be completed within thirty days from the 31st of March. It was the duty of the commissioner to revise all schedules before transmitting them to the central office. Ten per cent of all the schedules were in before the end of April; fifty-eight per cent before the end of May; eighty-three per cent before the end of June and ninety-five per cent before the end of July, and those that were not received before that date were in connection with the most remote districts of Canada. In 1891 only one per cent of the schedules was received before the end of April; forty-one per cent before the end of May; eighty-three per cent before the end of June and ninety-six per cent before the end of July. This shows a very considerably increased efficiency and a quicker return of the large bulk of the schedules in 1901 over 1891.
Will the minister repeat what percentage was returned at the end of July in 1891 ?

The return in July in both cases was practically the same, but that includes the ones that were sent in almost immediately, as well as those that were sent in in July, and if you take the earlier months you will find a much larger percentage in 1901 than in

1891. Naturally, at the eud there are always a large number that cannot be brought in earlier, those dealing with the outlying parts of the 'country, but in both cases the ones that could be brought in early were brought in earlier ; they were brought in early in 1901 and not so early In 1891.
'Mr. CLARICE. Might I ask the minister if the schedules containing the statistics respecting manufactures are included in the schedules, the date of the return of which he has just given ?
No ; in all cases, both in this and the other census, there was a special enumeration with respect to manufactures.
Have you the dates there when the schedules with respect to manufactures were finally received by your department ?

I will inquire about that. The first volume of the census of 1SD1 was issued March 20tli, 1893, or two years later ; it comprised 424 pages. The first volume of the census of 1901 was issued in December, 1902 and comprised 561 pages, including a great deal more information and a larger number of tables than were included in the first volume of the census of 1891. The second volume of the census of 1891 was issued on November 25, 1S93 ; the third, dealing with manufactures, on February 20tli, 1895, and the fourth, including agriculture, forest products and miscellaneous, appeared February 11, 1S97. Now, the second and third volumes of the census of 1901, dealing with agriculture, which was included only in the fourth volume of the census of 1891, with forest products, which was also the fourth volume of the census of 1891, and with fisheries, manufactures and mining, are now just about complete and will be in the hands of the printer next month. They include all the information that was in the second, third and fourth volumes of the census of 1891. The second volume of the census of 1891 was issued in November, 1893, about the same period as the second volume in the present census, but the third volume did not come out until two years after that, in 1895, and the fourth, dealing with agriculture, forest products and miscellaneous, not until 1897.
Now, as to bulletins. The first bulletin of the census of 1901, containing the population of some cities and towns, and also the populations of census districts for the years 1881 and 1891. is dated in August of 1891. The first bulletin of 1901, which is dated August also, gave the population by census districts, and in addition to what was given in the census of 1891, contained the number of families and the number of dwellings in each census district, together with the population of towns and cities according to their municipal boundaries. It appeared about the same date as the first bulletin in the Hon. Mr. FISHER.
other census, but it contained double the amount of information.
The first bulletin was issued about the same date ?
It was issued about the same date, but it contained double the amount of information.	.
Are we to understand that the census return for 1891 did not give the families at all ?
The families were not included in the bulletins ; they were in the subsequent volume, which was not issued until much later.
The first information received was issued about the same date ?
A certain proportion, about one-half of it. The bulletins of 1901 stated that in a few districts the records were incomplete.
You changed some figures?

Some figures were changed in both cases ; the bulletins were never absolutely complete when they were Issued in either case. They were compiled and issued for the information of the public from time to time, subject to revision, and in some cases subject to change. It was stated in the bulletin that they were not complete, because there were outlying districts of which the population and details were not contained in the bulletins, but that was the case in the bulletins both of 1901 and of 1891.
Several bulletins were issued, if my memory serves me ?

Several bulletins were issued. The first bulletin of the census of 1891 was issued in August ; the second, which was issued in October, gave the population Of Ontario ; the third, which was issued in November, gave the population of the maritime provinces by districts and sub-districts ; the fourth, which was issued hi December, gave the population of Quebec by districts and sub-districts ; the fifth, which was issued in February, 1892, gave, by districts and sub-districts, the population of 'Manitoba and the North-west Territories ; and the sixth, issued in February, contained a summary of the dwellings of the people.
In 1991 tlie first bulletin of the Census was issued in August and gave the population, the number of families and tlie number of dwellings by census districts, together with the population of cities and towns. It contained information which was included in the sixth bulletin of the former census. The second bulletin, issued on January 29tli, 1902. was delayed a little while for the full details of the information from the outlying territory.

When was the second
bulletin issued in 1S91 ?
In October.
Two mouths after the first [DOT]>
Yes.
How many months elapsed between the first and second bulletins in 1901 ?

From August to January-sijf months.
The second bulletin of the census of 1891 gave the population of Ontario by sub-districts, just the population of Ontario. The bulletin of the census of 1901 gave the whole population of Ontario and Manitoba, classed as rural and urban ; the population of all incorporated cities, towns and villages, situated in one census district, together with the details of population of all cities, towns and villages situated in two or more census districts.
Repeating what is in the first bulletin.
No, it does not. The third bulletin was issued January 22nd, and gave the same details of .population as the second, but gave them for Quebec and the maritime provinces.
What is the date of the issue of the third bulletin ?

Several days later than that of the second bulletin, practically they were issued at the same time, the one dealing with Ontario and Manitoba and the other dealing with Quebec and the maritime provinces. They were issued a week apart, giving information which was not contained in any of the bulletins that were issued in the census of ten years before.

You struck a new line ? The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE. Quite a new line ; we struck quite a number of new liifes ; if we had not, our census would have been a poor one.
The fourth gave the same information for British Columbia and the North-west Territories and the unorganized districts ; it was issued one week later. Practically those three bulletins were issued together, although they were a week apart.
How do the dates compare with the bulletins of 1891 1
In 1891 the date of those bulletins were October, November and December, but they did not contain the information to be found in the bulletins of 1901.
What were the dates in 1901 ?

December and January, but containing information which the other did not. No. 5 was issued on February the 21st and another two weeks later, giving the religion of the people bv provinces and territories, including 142 different specified religions, together with a comparative table of the two censuses. That was not given in any of the bulletins of the former census. The seventh issued in March gave the population of the Dominion by origin, which is not to be found in any of the bulletins of the former census. Bulletin eight issued on the 30th of April, gave the immigration and birth place, which was not included in any of the bulletins of the former census. Number six gave the population of the Dominion by sex and couiugal conditions on the 24tli of February. These bulletins were issued one after the other as rapidly as they could be obtained from the printer. Number seven was issued on the 12th of March, and number eight on the 30th of April. Number nine, issued on the 16th of April, gave the infirmities, also not given in any of the bulletins of the last census. Number ten, issued on the 25th of July, gave the census of the people by ages, which is not given in any of the bulletins of the former census. Number eleven, issued 24th of November, gave the agricultural statistics of Prince Edward Island-information which did not reach the people, in the census of 1891, until 1897, when four volumes of the census were issued, or six years after the information was obtained. But in the last census this information was given to the people by the bulletin of the 24th of November, 1902, or only eighteen months after it was got from the' people. On the 20th of December, the bulletin was issued giving the agricultural statistics of British Columbia. The bulletin of the 13tli of December gave the agricultural statistics of Nova Scotia. On the 14tli of December was issued the bulletin giving the agricultural statistics of the North-west Territories. On the 15th of December we had the agricultural statistics of Manitoba, and on the 16th those of New Brunswick. We now- have ready the agricultural statistics of the whole Dominion.
Are those of Ontario issued yet ?

No, nor of Quebec, but they are just going to the printer. This information was not given until after the issue of the fourth volume of the census of 1891, which was issued in 1897, or six years after the census was taken, whereas in the present instance we are giving the agricultural statistics of the Dominion within a little over two years from the time of taking the census.

The hon. gentleman gave us the date on which a certain number of the first bulletins of the census of 1901 were

issued. He did not give the dates of the others.

I gave you all. There were six. The hon. gentleman has spoken about a compilation. A few months ago, in discussing this matter, I said that there was a considerable amount of money spent in both these census on the fishery schedules. In the census of 1891 there was a considerable amount of money spent in taking information of that character, but when it was brought into the office here, it was found so incomplete and inaccurate that it was thrown aside and never compiled. We, however, compiled the information we got. While the census of 1901 has cost double as much as that of 1891, in the census of 1901 we have got information which is valuable and accurate, whereas in 1891 we did not get much information, and what we did get was largely inaccurate, owing to the careless and cheap way in which it was taken and compiled. Those things have to be taken into consideration when we make a comparison between the two censuses.
Did not the hon. gentleman invite the officer who had charge of the census of 1891 to assist in the completion of the census of 1901 ?

No, because I found that the results of the census of 1891 were so inaccurate and incomplete that I did not want the census of 1901 under the charge of that officer. Let me give an instance in confirmation of what I say. It Is well known that in the province of Quebec, they use the measure of the ar-pent and not the acre, a difference of about one-sixth, five acres being equal to about six arpents. It is also well known that in the province of Quebec the farmers measure their grain and other products by the minot and not the bushel. The minot 'is thirty-six pounds, while the standard bushel is thirty-four pounds. Well, in the taking of the agricultural census in the province of Quebec in 1891, the enumerators were instructed to take their information from the people as given in arpents and minots, and the change would be made in the office here, but I found that the figures of the census were exactly those given by the enumerators. What is the result 1 It is that a farmer of the province of Quebec, who had say 100 arpents of oats which would give say about 5,000 minots at 50 minots to the arpent was credited with 100 acres giving only 5.000 bushels, thus losing both ways for he had only 83 acres which gave nearly 5,300 bushels or nearly 64 bushels to the acre. Our farmers in the province of Quebec are thus discredited before the world, and it is shown that their crops are smaller though the area is larger; that their land is poorer, and so that they are but indifferent farmers. And that is a specimen of the way in which

the compilation of the census of 1891 was made in the statistical bureau of my department. This was before I became Minister of Agriculture. I did not wish to see that repeated in the census of 1901. I took care that the officer who allowed that to be done was not in charge of the census of 1901. Let me give but one or two items to show that the details in the schedules of 1891 did not correspond with the tables issued to the world. We have found many such cases, but I have not the details at my fingers' ends. Nor do I wish to occupy the time of the House in giving a mass of details when a few citations will suffice. The first case to which I would refer is in the county of Addington in Ontario. The statistics with regard to this district show products in 1891 largely in excess of those shown by the schedule of 1901. In this, as in so many other cases, we were obliged to go into details in order to account for an extraordinary comparison and to learn why the figures showed lack of progress in parts of the country where we knew the progress had been phenomenal between the last census and this one. We first revised our own figures to see if errors had been made there. Finding no error, we went back to the schedules of 1891. And what did we find ? We found the case of one flour nTill alone credited with an output of $560,000 in 1891. This was one single flour mill. We found that, whereas the schedule of the enumerators showed that this mill had two employees, the table made in the department showed six. The amount paid in wages, according to the enumerator's schedule, was $750, but this had been changed to $3,750 in the office here in Ottawa. The value of raw material was changed from $45,000 to $420,000-a trifle of nearly ten times. The value of the product was given as $600,000, the product being entered in the enumerator's schedule in written numbers as three million pounds. Now, three million pounds of mill products, as everybody knows, is not worth $600,000. The value of it could not reasonably exceed $60,000. No doubt, a larger sum was given by error of the enumerator. The owner of the mill states in a letter that for eighteen years his product has been about 60 barrels of flour per day. The revision failed there in not going back to the original source of information. We did go to the original source of information and made corrections in the case of manifest and obvious inaccuracies of the schedules. Now here was another case. In 1891, Montreal Centre is credited-at page 88, vol.
3 of the census of 1891-with a cartridge factory having a working capital of $175,000. employing 90 persons, paying $30,000 in wages per year, using $100,000 worth of raw material, and having a total output of $200,000. Now. there never was a cartridge factory in Montreal Centre. A certain cartridge factory, situated in Brownsburg, in

the county of Argenteuil, has its office in. the city of Montreal. But that office was credited with the factory and all the details, and all were repeated in Argenteuil county, ail counted double.
And all paid for.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: And paid for double. Now, I will not go at greater length into these matters, but I will say a few words as to the accusation of my hon. friend (Mr. Blain) that we have departed from the rate of pay and the rules of payment.
If the minister will excuse me, I think he has forgotten to show the number employed in compiling the census in 1891 and 1901.
I cun give that now
I think it would be better; the comparison can be given with greater convenience.

I am not certain that I have the number employed, but I have the cost of compilation for the two years. The salaries which were paid, independent of the enumerators, for the census of 1901 amounted to $236,731. That includes not only the compilers, but the chief officers of the census and all the salary connected with the census apart from the enumeration in the country. For the census of 1891 the same items amounted to $121,000-here again a little over half what it was in 1901. I think I have already given evidence how it was that it could be done for that amount at that time. My hon. friend (Mr. Blain) spoke about the expense of telegraphing. I have not the figures in sufficient detail to show the expense of telegraphing by itself. But I have the figures of ' sundries,' which includes telegrams, travelling expenses of the head office staff, and things of that kind. In the census of 1901 this item cost $9,300, and in the census of 1891 the same item cost $17,000, or nearly double. So, in that respect, at all events, we were not extravagant.
Now, I wish to say a few words on the subject on which I had begun to speak when the hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule) interrupted me. My hon. friend (Mr. Blain) has accused me of departing from the schedule of rates and making payments extraneous to the proper payments. I plead guilty to that quite frankly. I say freely that the schedule of rates was fixed for ordinary circumstances, there were cases in which the circumstances were extraordinary and called for special consideration, and which were given special consideration, and in which an exception was made in order to make payments larger than the ordinary schedule of rates would permit.
Such conditions as the peculiar enlargement of the work which a man had to do, and over a greater territory ; peculiar conditions where he had to do the work over again in consequence of something for which he was in no wise at fault ; peculiar conditions such as the one mentioned in the House before, where the papers in a whole district were lost by accident to a ship, and the work had to be done all over again ; other peculiar conditions where the increased expenditure was vouched for as being proper and legitimate, and it was shown clearly by vouchers that the officer had really expended the money. In this connection I would like to draw attention to the fact that the Auditor General has not objected to tiie passing of a single account coming from my department. I think therefore we may fairly conclude that the accounts were subjected to a proper audit and a proper scrutiny. Now my hon. friend would leave the House and the country to suppose that in the other census the schedule of rates was absolutely adhered to, wliefeas we have departed from it. He has assumed that it was impossible, under the holy and good Conservative party, that anything of that kind could have been done, but that as soon as the horrible Grits came into office we were guilty of all these naughty things. Well. Sir, I am charitable, I wish to believe that my predecessors in office found the same kind of difficulties that I found, and found that there were peculiar conditions and circumstances-
Not so many of them.

Perhaps not, but I have found that while the schedule of rates under my predecessors applied to the whole work, there were a great many exceptions, and there were cases where, in justice to an efficient officer, they had to make allowance and give greater pay. I plead guilty to having done that thing in a good many cases. But I want to give a few instances in which my 'predecessors did the same thing in the census of 1891, and I think my hon. friend will acknowledge that if they were justified in departing from the schedule of rates in 1891, I may have been actuated by equally proper motives in desiring to do justice to the employees of the government. I will take the county of Addington, Ontario, as being first on the list. I find that out of twenty enumerators, there were no less than five who were paid considerably higher than the schedule of rates would allow. For instance, there wras one man who was entitled by the schedule to $37.15, and who was paid $54, a flat rate of $3 a day for eighteen days, contrary to the law, and contrary to the schedule of rates. But I have no doubt that some good reason for that expenditure appeared which justified the department. By the next item I find that where the schedule of rates would have given a man $12.72, he was paid $27, a little

more than double. Another man should have got $51.30, he was paid $69. Another mail should have got $24.75, he was paid $42.
Would the minister give us the cost of taking the census of Addington on the two occassions.

Speaking roughly, I suppose it was about double on the last occasion, I will assume that for the sake of argument, and plead guilty to it. In the county of North Bruce, for which I have the list here, I find that, contrary to the schedule of rates, men were paid by the flat rate of $3 a day, contrary to law, contrary to the accounts they ought to have supplied and sworn to. The first case I find is where a man should have been paid $28.64 by the schedule of rates and be was paid $45 ; in another case he should have been paid $41.58 and he was paid $54. So on down the list every one of them was paid contrary to the law and more than the schedule of rates allowed. Now take the county of Frontenac here I find the same thing. One man ought to have got $48.31, and he was paid $3 a day for eighteen days, $54. Another man ought to have got $21.45, and he was paid for eight days at $3 a day, $24. Another man ought to have got $5.45, and he was paid for eight days at $3 a day, $24. In the county of Peterborough East I find the same kind of thing. Ten of the enumerators were paid more than the tariff of rates allowed them, were paid contrary to law, for so many days at $3 a day. The same was true, to a certain extent, in North Renfrew. Also I find that in Simcoe East- where is my hon. friend from East Simcoe (Mr. Bennett) V-all the enumerators in 1891 were paid a flat rate of $3 a day. contrary to law and contrary to the tariff of rates which was then issued. In North Renfrew nearly all of them were paid in the same way. The hon. member who then represented South Renfrew seems to have had a little more influence with the minister than the hon. member for Simcoe. because he no't only got $3 a day for twenty-five days for the enumerators of his county, but he also got an extra five cents on every farm they enumerated, an extra ten cents over the schedule of rates on every factory and industrial establishment they enumerated. The same is true of South Waterloo, where every one of the enumerators, contrary to the law, contrary to the tariff of rates, was paid $3 for more days than the tariff would have allowed them to get. The same in North Waterloo.
Now. Mr. Speaker, I need not go further into details, as I could if I had tfme. While I admit that the census this time has cost double as much. I believe we have got returns for the money spent. I believe we have got an accurate census, giving information that will be much more valuable to students of economics in Canada. I believe that we can show a census by which every Hon. Mr. FISHER.
part of the Dominion is fairly represented, unlike the census of 1891 where the province of Quebec was misrepresented, to the detriment of that province, to the discredit of the people of that province, to the discredit of a large number of industrious agriculturists and inhabitants throughout this Dominion.	We have got reliable
information, and I venture to say that the information which is given in the census of 1901 will be found accurately to tally* with the totals and the compilations which have been made up from it, because in addition to the compilers, we have had a staff of revisers who have been going over the work once, twice and in many cases three times, so as to insure perfect accuracy. My hon. friend has complained of the increased number of employees engaged on this census. It is true we have had more employees, it is true we have been spending more in the compilation, but, as I have shown, when our compilation is finished it is correct, it is absolutely right and complete, instead of being left incomplete and unfinished as is was in 1891.
It was because your work was badly done.

No, my hon. friend (Mr. Pope) is entirely mistaken. If he would go to the schedule of 1891 and compare them as we have been comparing them with the -compilations he would find that the schedules of 1891 did not tally with the compilations in many instances and -that the work was done in a slovenly and incomplete manner; whereas, under our arrangement the work has been revised and checked and gone over so as to make it absolutely accurate and correct. I venture to say that in statistical work there is one thing that is absolutely necessary and that is accuracy. Statistical work without accuracy is absolutely useless and unfortunately the statistical work of this census will lose to a certain extent its value by reason of the fact that comparisons between the results of the census of 1891 and the results of the census of 1901 are not fair or proper comparisons because the census of 1891 was so inaccurate and incomplete. I venture to think that in the census of 1901 we have made a new departure, that we have done some new thing, that we have done a thing which I hope and believe will be the beginning of accurate statistics in the Dominion of Canada and that as a result of the taking of this -census the people will be able when the time comes .to take further statistics to make proper and accurate comparisons with this census, the deductions from which will be of value in the economic study of the condition of the country. Believing this and believing that I have made out a case which cannot be impugned in any way I will rest satisfied that the House will vote down the resolution of my hon. friend.

Mr. Speaker, I only desire to occupy a few moments to consider 'the question which has been handled by the hon. Minister of Agriculture (Hon. Mr. Fisher) and X want to take up the last statement that he made first. He said :	We got thorough and reliable
information while the census of 1891 was entirely unreliable and inaccurate. What evidence have we of the statement that we have reliable information ? We have simply his bare statement unsupported by any proofs. We might just as well believe from the knowledge we have that the census of 1891 is correct as that the census of 1901 is correct. If the hon. Minister of Agriculture cannot support his statement by any better proof than that which he has presented then I say the country can fairly be allowed to judge how far it should give credence to such a statement. In reference to the census of 1901 he admits that the same work cost more than double what it did in 1891. What explanation does lie give of that additional cost and what justification lias he given for it '! We know that as a party economy was always their cry but as a government extravagance was always their practice. This is another illustration of it and it is as good a one as we have had for quite a length of time. To what does he attribute tile increased cost ? First, the .increased cost is attributed to the increased cost of labour and secondly to the Increase in the amount of work done. He says that the census of 1891 did not entail as much work as the census of 1901, that labour was higher, that the cost of living was greater ; therefore it is natural that the census would cost more. First then in regard to the cost of labour, what evidence have we of it ? I endeavoured to satisfy myself upon that and X took up the figures which the labour bureau has compiled- in regard to the cost of wages in 1901. It is true that you cannot very readily make a comparison as to the cost of this class of labour because it does not give a statement regarding the cost of labour in this line, tout one line that would serve as a comparison is the cost of labour. The cost would be proportionately about the same in the two lines. I take the cost of labour according to the ' Labour Gazette' in 1901, and I will compare the wage of the ordinary labourer in 1901 with what it was in 1891 because that is the only class of labour for which I can find a statement in both years. I find that the ordinary labourer in 1901 got from $1 to $1.25 per day. The average of that would be $1,124 a day. I take up the report of the Bureau of Statistics for the province of Ontario and I find that the ordinary farm labourer received in 1891, boarding himself, $25.81 a month throughout the whole province. The farm labourer cannot work every day in the month so that $25.81 is really more than $1 a day for every day he worked, so that if we credit him with the additional earnings he would have received, he must have got at least $1.12| a day, while the average rate of wages in 1901 was $1,124 a day. Is that an evidence that there was much difference in the price of labour in both decades ? It is an evidence that the price of labour was comparatively the same, that there was very little difference and that therefore the increased cost of labour could not account for the increased expense of taking the Census. Then, in the next place the hon. minister says:	We did a great deal more work.
Well, it is true that there was a little more work done but I find that in giving an answer to the hon. member for Peel as to how much more work was done the hon. minister said that the number of questions that were asked in 1891 was 2,111,136, while *the number of questions asked in 1901 was 3,034,000, or practically not quite one-third more questions asked while there was double the expense. The wages were practically the same in both decades but the work was done by one set of men in 1891 and toy another in 1901. Is there evidence that the increased cost of labour or the increase in the amount of work can fairly account for the increased cost ? I say that neither accounts for it. While we would naturally expect that the census of 1901 would cost a fraction more than the census of 1891, I say that the additional expense is out of all proportion to the additional work that was done. That cannot account for it, and I say that nothing does account for it except extravagance and blundering as far as I can see. The hon. Minister of Agriculture says :	We have done this work
over two or three times. It was only because they were not satisfied in the first place that it was correct, which compelled them to do their work over and over again in order to make it presentable to the public. It required to be examined and checked by some independent authority and therefore I would not be disposed to take the hon. minister's statement as satisfactory evidence of its accuracy without examining it itself. I will take the work that was done in my county. In two ridings of Grey there was a decrease in population as between 1891 and 1901. Take the east riding of Grey which I have the honour to represent. In 1S91 there was a population of 26,225 and in 1901 a population of 25,387 or a decrease of 838. In the first instance 26 enumerators, the commissioner and all, were required to take the census while in the second instance 59 were required to do the same work; or in other words 29 more men were employed in 1901 to do the work that was done in 1891.
In 1891 the census in that riding cost $1,834, and in 1901 it cost $3,592, or nearly double. That shows that the men employed by this government in 1901 were incompetent, or extravagant, or unbusinesslike, and perhaps all three combined. They can impale themselves on which horn of the di-

lemma they like. The officials in 1891 did . the work as accurately as the officials in 1891, and they did it for $1,659 less money. In 1891, in North Grey, twenty-six men were employed, at a cost of $1,665, to take the census, and in 1901, with a population of 1,000 more than 1891, fifty-one men were employed, at a cost of $3,000, or again nearly double. In South Grey, in 1891, twenty-three men took the census of a population of 23,672 people at a cost of $1,047, hut in 1901 it took thirty-nine men to take the census of 22,171, or 1,500 fewer of a population, and it cost $2,591, or $844 more than in 1891. This shows that the same work was done much more economically in 1891, than in 1901, and in every respect the work was as well done. It is true that perhaps one-third more questions were asked in 1901 than in 1891, and if the increased cost had only been one-third more, there perhaps would be no serious objection ; but the fact remains that the cost of the census in 1901 was nearly double the cost of the census of 1891 in every instance. The Minister of Agriculture told us, that he wanted more men employed because he wanted the returns within a shorter time, but the truth is, that in the main the census figures of 1891, were got out as early as those of 1901. The minister did not supply the census to the people of the country very much earlier in 1901 than they were supplied in 1891. I asked the Minister of Agriculture for a comparison between the number employed in compiling the census in 1891 with the number employed in 1901. He dare not give the figures, because the difference in number is so much greater in 1901 that he was ashamed of if. Although I honestly believe that he had the information under his hand, he dared not give it to the House notwithstanding that I asked him three times for it.
Some lion. MEMBERS. Order.
I am perfectly in order. The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE. What does the hon. gentleman refer to ?

I said that the hon. minister dare not make a comparison between the number employed in compiling the census in 1891 and the number employed in 1901, because the difference was so great in the latter year that he was ashamed of it.

I gave the hon. gentleman the cost. The numbers vary from time to time. There was a certain staff in the beginning on both compilations, and that staff was reduced from time to time. So that it would be very difficult to give any figures.
Would it be difficult to give the number of days they were employed ?

I would have to make a calculation as to Hon. Mr. FISHER.
that, and that calculation I have not under my hand, and the hon. gentleman has no right to say I have.

I do not desire to make any charge against the minister that I cannot prove, but I do say, that if he wanted to make a fair comparison he could have given us the number of days of work. Although I have asked for this information several times during the session, I have never been able to get it, and I have the right to assume that for some reason or other unknown to me, he desires to keep that information to himself. I say that from the first to the last, an examination of this census proves that the government have done the work in an extravagant fashion. I shall not say that it was done incompetently, because I would require more detailed information to justify that statement, but I do say that no reason has been given to this House, to show that the census of 1901 is any more correct than the census of 1891. I do know for a fact, with regard to my own locality, that the census was not accurately taken in 1901.
Mr. HEYI). Give us the facts.

I am stating the fact from my own personal knowledge, as to my own locality, and I may fairly draw the inference that the same remark applies to other localities. I therefore say that the minister cannot justify the claim that he has given us an accurate census. When we endeavoured to bring these schedules before the Public Accounts Committee, the minister dared not allow them to be presented before that committee. I leave the country to draw the inference why that was the case. The Minister of Agriculture took the responsibility of instructing his officers to keep from the committee the information which the committee was entitled to by precedent and practice, and I can only reach the conclusion that that was done to prevent us from making the facts known to the people of the country. The hon. gentleman has no reason to congratulate himself upon the magnificent work he has done in taking the census. He has done the same work as his predecessors, but It has cost the country twice as much money and the country has secured nothing that will compensate it for a fraction of the difference in cost. '

One would have thought that after seven months our friends on the other side would have been able to make out a stronger case than they have done. They have been endeavouring to deceive the people, not only in this House, but throughout the length and breadth of the country, on this great question of the census. They have been issuing from the parliament buildings here, franked to all parts of the country, charges against the government with respect to the census which convinces me that they will try to

make this an issue before the people. A document with respect to the census which they have circulated, and which has come into my hands, is absolutely misleading and untrue in almost every particular. I have looked over it with a considerable degree of care and have put on the Order Paper three questions in order to give the census authorities an opportunity of answering three charges which are made in the paper. 1 will read them to show the House the character of the matter they are supplying to the people, and that absolute worthlessness of what is contained in their literature. It says :
At one time a staff of thirty men worked for months on enumerators' accounts. Then a new basis was applied and all their work thrown away.
The answer of the Census Department to this is :
The statement is absolutely untrue in every particular.
They make a further statement :
A year's work was done by a large staff on mortality tables which were all condemned and burned ; after which the work was done over again. The same thing happened to other compilations.
The Census Department say, in answer to this :
The work on the mortality tables has been done by four clerks and no part of the work has been condemned or burnt. The statement is wholly untrue.
And I will say what the commissioner would not dare to say, that it is an absolutely false statement, calculated to deceive the people. The third statement contained in this sheet, and these are specimens of the work, is this :
For about two years a staff of about thirty persons have been engaged in altering and amending enumerators' returns, changing forest land to pasture land, fallow land to pasture, and making other alterations.
The reply to this statement is that, it is absolutely untrue in every particular. The word ' fallow ' brings to my mind the fact that tlie only charge against the census that is made here to-day, after seven months' work, is that there is not a column in the schedules for fallow land. I think tlie opposition ought to have prepared a better attack. We have had two or three fallow years in which these gentlemen could have prepared themselves to make some real attack against the government and the quality of this census. We -have the work, we can analyse it for ourselves, and we can see whether the census for 1901 was a good census and whether it was an improvement on the census of 1891, yet the only suggestion that our friend from Peel threw out was that the municipal assessors should make this census. This, he said, would he a great saving to the people. In
the city of Brantford we have two assessors and it takes them six months to make an assessment of the city of Brantford. How long would it take tlie two assessors of tlie city of Brantford to take the census, when it took twenty-two men thirty days ? It would take them two years at the least, and the whole advantage of a census is that it is taken quickly and covers a great deal of ground.
But tlie principal charge is that this census is too expensive, and they try to prove that by the statement that the census of 1891 cost less than that of 1901. The fact that the census of 1901 cost nearly $1,200,000, is no evidence at all of extravagance, nor is there any evidence of economy in the census of 1891, because it cost only $550,000. If I was to say that I built a house in 189.1 for $1,000, and that I built another in 1901 and it cost me $3,000, and then claimed that there was economy In the building of 1891 and extravagance in 1901, every one would see the absurdity of the position. If a man said :	I ran my factory in 1891 for $500
per annum, and last year it cost me three times ns much, the first question the ordinary man would ask is : Have yon the same character of work and the same quantity of work in 1901 as you had in 1891 V For purpose of comparison we must have things that are similar. A man who would compare the census of 1891 with the census of 1901 would thereby show that he had not looked into the character of the census. There is no comparison in the completeness of the two, or the amount of labour involved in securing the information. Let us take the number of men engaged. In 1891 there were only 4,324 while in 1901 there were 8,800, more than double the number of men to take census. But it is not the same census. It is a much more complete census involving a great deal more labour, and for that very reason
Wherein is tlie eeusus of 1001 more complete in respect to Ontario than that of 1891 ?

I understand that the remuneration per name was 3 cents in 1891 and 5 cents in 1901. It seems to me that 5 cents is very cheap for the work done. It has been said in this House that it cost a certain newspaper in Montreal more than 5 cents a head to get the signatures attached to certain petitions to this House. Now whether they got 3 cents or 5 cents does not prove anything.
Do you know that ?

There are a good many things I know that I cannot say here, and there are certain things I ought to say which, being what I consider myself, a gentleman, I would not say. Now let us compare the work that the enumerator was expected to do for 3 cents in 1S91 with what he was expected to do for 5 cents in

1901. We liave the evidence of that in the number of questions there were asked. I have certain schedules here ; I took them up indiscriminately, and they do not cover the whole work, hut they will illustrate my point. We have the great factor that the enumerators in 1901 had eleven schedules besides four specials, while in 1891 there were only nine. The population has also in-ereased, so that there is a greater amount of work. But leaving that aside, let us take the schedules dealing with land and farms, one of which would be in the hands of almost every enumerator. The number of questions asked in 1891 was seventy-five, while in 1901 it was 127. We could hardly expect one man to take as many names when he had to ask 127. questions as he would take when he had to ask only seventy-five. Let us take the schedules dealing with manufactures of clay. In those the number of questions is not so material as the statistical work that is afterwards involved. In 1891 there were ten columns, while in 1901 there were thirty-one columns, and the necessary clerical work of classifying this additional number involved the expenditure of an exceedingly large sum of money.
Take the question of minerals, which is a very important part of the exports of this country and deserves exceptional treatment. In 1891, the exports of our mineral products only amounted to $5,748,000, while in 1901, they amounted to $40,000,000. That certainly justifies the hon. Minister of Agriculture in spending a little more money to secure a proper return upon the mineral resources of the country. In the census of 1891, there were only twenty-three questions on this subject, while there were 224 in 1901. How could you expect the census enumerators in British Columbia to take down for the same price the answers to 224 questions which their predecessors charged, who only had to answer 23. Could you expect the department to compile, separate, analyse and compute the figures and put them in suitable shape in the case of the returns to 224 questions as yon would in the case of the replies to 23. Yet we have the government charged with extravagance because the work in each case was not done at the same price. Take the question of manufactures ; manufacturing in Canada has grown to enormous proportions. In the schedule of 1891, there were only 23 questions, whereas in that of 1901 there were 63. How could you expect the work to be done in both cases for the same price, more especially when you consider the additional work involved in the collation and compilation of the returns and the additional number of enumerators who had to be employed. In 1891 our exports only amounted to $6,000,000 whereas in 1901 they amounted to $18,000,000. Any information that shows the development of our agricultural, mineral and manufacturing resources, the people will not begrudge paying for ; and if the census of
1901 has cost $1,250,000, as compared with $500,000 for 1891, the people have got good value for their money. Take the articles of butter and cheese ; in 1891 the exports of cheese amounted to $9,000,000, and in 1901 to $19,886,000. Butter in 1891 was exported to the value of $602,000, and in 1901, the export amounted to $5,600,000. In 1891 very few questions were asked regarding this industry, whereas a great many were asked in 1901. Take the schedule on population, there are on it thirty-four questions compared witli sixteen in 1891, or eighteen new ones. That involves additional work in compiling the returns and the engaging of additional clerks. Take clay, thirty-one questions were asked in 1901 against ten in 1891. Then take minerals, in 1891 the questions were twenty-eight, and in 1901, 200. I need scarce-t ly allude to the subject of fisheries, concerning which there are over 200 questions. There are over 100 more in 1901 than in 1891. And the fishery industry is an important one in this country, one in which a large number of men find a livelihood, and the government, in spending money to gain information for the people with regard to that industry, did just what they ought to have done under the circumstances. Hon. gentlemen on the other side are comparing two things that are entirely dissimilar, the census of 1891 and the census of 1901. I have here two books, one the first volume of the census of 1891, and the other the first volume of the census of 1901. An examination of these two will show that hon. gentlemen opposite are not properly informed and are simply indulging in a little captious criticism. There is no comparison of the quality of the information contained in the two volumes. If you take the first volume of the census of 1891, you will find 105 pages taken up with this class of information, as shown by the headings :
Houses-wood, brick, stone ; houses-1 story, 2 stories. 3 stories, 4 stories and over ; houses- 1 room, 2 rooms. 3 rooms, 4 rooms, 5 rooms, 6 to 10 rooms, 11 to 15 rooms, 16 rooms and over, uninhabited, in construction.
The last two are of importance. But for 105 pages out of 375 we have information of the class indicated by the headings I have read. What do the people of this country care how many houses of one storey, or two stories, or three stories there are ? What do they care how many houses there are of one, two, six or fifteen rooms ? That is not information of any particular value to the people. When you come to the heading ' civil condition of the people,' they use 104 pages, but the information is woefully incomplete as compared with the census of 1901. Then when you take religion, you find 105 pages devoted to it. A great many of our people attach a great deal of importance to religion, and in this volume of 1901 there are 140 pages devoted to the subject. Then take tjie division ' plaee of birth.' We take a great deal of interest in

the question of where our people come from, and are spending large amounts of money every year to bring into our country the best class of people. The census of 1891 has 31 pages devoted to origin and nationality, while in 1901 we have 190 pages. And yet our friends on the other side say that this 190 pages of high class statistical work is to be done at the same rate as the 31 pages of the census of 1891. Why, the thing is absurd on the face of it. In the first volume of the census of 1891 there were only 89 subjects dealt with, while in 1901 there were 201, or nearly three times as many. There is exactly three times as much information, judging from the number of columns. Then take the matter of quality. There are seven schedules here or heads covered in 1891, while in 1901 there were 18. There are about only 215 questions to answer in 1891, while in 1901 there are over 523 questions. And yet our friends accuse us of extravagance because we cannot get up such an elaborate census as this at the same cost as that of the census of 1891. If you show that a .man spent $3,000 in running his factory in 1891 and $10,000 in 1901, you do not show that he has necessarily failed in economical management. It may be that he has more employees and is turning out more work. The only fault I find with the Minister of Agriculture is that he did not pay the claims of these men who put in good hard work and did not get enough for it. I say that at 5 cents .per name it was impossible to get that information and cover long distances and earn fair wages. And while the census of 1901 did cost more, the men were not as well paid and did not earn as much money as ten years before. If the Auditor General's Report shows that they got $3 a day, they never received it. Those in my constituency were not paid $3 a day. The number of names they took was divided by 60 and that gave the number of days, and each of them were short from two to as high as fifteen or twenty days. That is where the trouble comes in for us, and trouble in which our lion, friends opposite are not interested. We will have to settle that with our enumerators. Some of them grumble, but they are too loyal to the country to be seduced from allegiance to their own party, though they were not so well paid as those who were appointed ten years before. When you look at the quantity of work, as shown by the two volumes I have here, you will see that the census for 1901 might as well have cost three times as much as that of 1891. In the census of 1891 there are only 83 columns, while in .that of 1901 there are over 200 devoted to statistical work. If hon. gentlemen opposite have more to say on the census, let them adduce facts. It is no argument to tell us that the cost is greater or that more men were employed. The question is what did the men do in 1901 and what did they do ten years before ?
Let them compare the result, and we shall be in a position to judge whether there has been any unwise expenditure or not. It does not prove anything for the hon. member for Peel to show that it cost more to take the census in his county in 1901 than it did in 1891. It cost more to run a hundred-acre farm in his county in 1901 than it did to run a fifty-acre farm ten years ago. You must compare things that are similar. Having given some attention to the question of the census, and having studied the American census, 1 devoted a little of my time since Saturday to looking into this matter, and I have found facts that .satisfied me that the government were not extravagant in taking this census ; while, on the other hand, I find that the census will answer the requirements of the people and give useful information. The charges made are not in accordance with the facts. And that is true of the charges contained in the campaign document of hon. gentlemen opposite which has been sent out from this House by the carload, by the train load. And I hope that those gentlemen of honour and respectability who sit on the other side-and there are many of them-instead of allowing such documents to go out by hundreds of thousands-and some destroyed because they are not untruthful enough-will take only ten minutes to look into the matter, and that will convince them that nearly every statement made in this campaign literature with regard to the census of 1901 is absolutely untrue.

I shall not detain the House long. The case has been so well presented by my hon. friend from Peel (Mr. Blain), who lias given a good deal of consideration to the question, and who, I think, has made out a very strong case for the resolution he has placed in your hands, that I need not dwell upon the matter at length. With reference to the leading argument of the hon. member for South Brant (Mr. Heyd), I find that he does not agree with the Minister of Agriculture. Tile minister was candid enough to tell us at the outset that the .main reason for the increase in the expense of taking the census was the higher cost of living. But the hon. member for South Brant, not being satisfied with that, endeavoured to show by a series of quotations from the various schedules of the census that there was an increase in the amount of work, that the volumes issued were larger and contained more information, and that this was the cause of the increase in the cost of taking the census. I will leave these two hon. gentlemen to settle this matter - between themselves. The hon. member for South Brant instances the taking of the censuses in cheese factories as a reason why there should be an increase in the expenditure. Now, if I understand it right, the mode of



taking tlie census of a factory requires the manager of the factory to be supplied, with schedules that he tills up, and practically the enumerator would not be employed for three minutes, much lfess for one day, in talcing that census.
Would it not involve more expense in the statistical branch ?

Well, I will explain that. If a cheese factory turned out 100,000 pounds of cheese in 1891, and in 1901 it turned out 200,000 pounds, I would' like to know by what course of reasoning my hon. friend from Brant (Mr. Heyd) anaves at the conclusion that the cost of taking a census of 200,000 pounds should be double that of taking the census of 100.000 pounds. I fail to see that the cost even of making the totals, of adding up these various reports of the cheese factories, would be any more in 1901 than it was in 1891. Possibly there might be a few more factories, but that would not account for doubling the cost of taking the census, which the Minister of Agriculture has confessed to.
The Minister of Agriculture tells us that one reason for the increased cost of taking the census on this last occasion was the employment of a larger number of enumerators, and consequently there was a larger number to be instructed. I think he is quite correct, and that is just what we complain of. He employs two or three times the number of people to take the census, these men all have to be instructed, and every one has to be paid his day's wage during the course of instruction-not only his day's wage, but I find, in some instances, that he is actually paid for his board. Some enumerators are given lunches when they meet together, as they were in VerchSres and Ohambly, down in the province of Quebec. Why were not the enumerators treated to lunches in my county as well ? I do not know why there should be any partiality shown. It goes to show the extreme carelessness with which these accounts are made up, when I found that in one county a man is allowed for an item that in another county another man is not allowed for.
Now, the Minister of Agriculture complains that in the census of 1891 the law was not complied with, and that enumerators were paid on a flat rate instead of by the day. I want to draw attention to this, because I think that in making that argument the minister was not as fair as he generally attempts to be. He took for example the county of Addington, the county of North Bruce, the county of North Renfrew, and the county of Frontenac. Now, we all know that these are counties where the population is sparse, where the enumerator in many instances would have to travel long distances between settlements in order to find the people living in that section of the country. But the Minister of Agri-Mr. HENDERSON.
culture did not mention a county like Peel, which is more thickly populated; like the county of Halton, which is well populated ; he made his reference entirely to counties that are sparsely settled, and where it would be an absolute necessity, to be fair to his enumerator, that some other plan should be adopted than that which would apply to counties with more dense population. I would not be surprised, if he analysed his own pay-sheets, if he found the figures to bear out my contention. Therefore, I think his argument in that respect was somewhat misleading. However, I fail to see that there is much in it, because he has told us that the cost of taking this census is practically double that of taking the former census, and I presume that it was doubled in those counties that he mentioned as well as in other counties.
Now, the Minister of Agriculture tells us that the cost of taking the census per name was three cents in 1891 and that was not enough. In 1901 he allows his enumerators five cents, an increase of 66f per cent for taking names. For taking farms, in 1891, the cost was 15 cents, and in 1901, 25 cents, still maintaining the same rate of increase, 06 per cent. Then, for taking the census of a factory, 20 cents was paid in 1891, and 30 cents in 1901, an increase of 50 per cent.
Now, he tells us that this increase was all owing to the extra cost of living. I wondered, when I heard him say that, where the boasted preferential tariff came in. Why, these hon. gentlemen were going to make everything cheap, they were making this a cheap country to live in, giving us cheap clothing, cheap food, cheap boots and shoes, everything the people have to buy was going to be cheap on account of this preferential tariff. Yet they tell us that they have had to pay their census enumerators more because the cost of living has been increased. What is the increase ? Did, the Minister of Agriculture, before he made that statement, look at the facts ? I doubt very much if he has; I think he has just spoken in a random sort of way. The Minister of Justice told us the other day that the salaries of the judges had to be increased because the cost of living had increased1, and they had to pay more for clothing and other requisites. But this preferential tariff, they told us, would make clothing cheap, that it would make boots and shoes in this country cheap to the consumer. I cannot reconcile the two arguments. Let me take some particular item and ask where the cost of living has been increased. Let me take as a basis of the whole thing the price of what. I look upon wheat as being a fair index of the respective cost of living in 1891 and 1901, because, to my mind, as the price of wheat varies so would the price of butter, so would the price of eggs and other articles that we consume. If the cost of wheat was less in 1891 than 1901 than would

be la 1901, and there would be something in the argument of the hon. gentleman. But what do I find ? Since the hon. gentleman made that statement about the cost of living being increased within the decade, a statement that almost staggered me, I went into the library and looked up the ' Globe ' newspaper to see what wheat sold for under the Conservative regime of 1891, when the farmers of this country enjoyed good government, when their interests were carefully looked after by the government of the day. I find that in 1891 wheat was selling for $1.08 per bushel, whereas in 1901 it is selling for the miserable price of 77 cents, 30 cents less. Yet the hon. gentleman tells us that he has had to pay his enumerators more because of the increased cost of living, a difference of 60 per cent, while the cost of wheat was reduced by 30 per cent. Does that not mean extravagance ? Is that not evidence sufficient to condemn the hon. gentleman out of his own mouth for the large amount that the census has cost ? I contend that the facts d'o not at all bear out his contention that the increased cost of living is the reason for the increased cost of taking the census. We may take other articles just as well as wheat. Take woollen goods. Under the preferential tariff hon. gentlemen opposite told us that the people were going to get their woollen goods cheaper. The complaint of the woollen manufacturers is that their industry has been destroyed by reason of the preferential tariff, which makes clothing cheaper, but it appears that the preferential tariff does not give the benefit to the consumer at all. It must .give it to the importer or middleman. 1 do not think they have reduced the cost to the consumer, because, the Minister of Agriculture tells us, the cost of living has increased. Therefore, the preferential tariff is not at all what the people expected it would be and does not result in the benefits that we hoped would accrue from it. j Until the hon. minister has given us a bet- i ter reason than the increased cost of living to justify this enormous increase in the cost of taking the census, this extravagant cost of taking the census. I shall be compelled, for one, to vote condemnation of his action, of the policy that he adopted and of the result of what he did in 1901.

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Henderson) who has just taken his seat has made a somewhat laboured argument to try and prove that the cost of living has not increased and that there should be no additional expense connected with the cost of taking the census. Whether the cost of- living has kept up to the price of wheat or not, I think that the hon. gentleman will admit that the cost of labour has increased. I venture to make the assertion, that, taking his own personal expenses as a criterion he will admit in 430}
private conversation, if not publicly, that the cost of living has very materially increased. If he will take up the volume of the census he will find an explanation of some of the reasons for the increased cost of taking it. The explanation was given by the hon. Minister of Agriculture (Hon. Mr. Fisher), and it was enlarged upon by him, so that it is not necessary to go into that. But, I simply want to allude to the fact that hon. gentlemen opposite can be all things to all men. They can adapt themselves to any condition of circumstances. It is not necessary to bring the tariff question into the discussion at the present ; but we have heard a good deal in this House in the past from hon. gentlemen opposite as to there being no advantage under the preferential tariff. We have been told by hon. gentlemen opposite that the preference was a delusion and a snare, and that we were imposing upon the people of the motherland as well as upon our own people in trying to convince them that there was some advantage in the preference. The hon. member for Halton (Mr. Henderson), by his extravagant language, and extravagant manner has admitted what the Liberals believe and have always contended, that the preference has been a decided advantage to the people. However, that is neither here nor there, as far as the census is concerned. We, on this side of the House, are prepared to admit that the cost of the census of 1901 has been greater than the cost of the census of 1891, and that was the only point made by the hon. member for Pe*l (Mr. Blain). Without being disrespectful to him at all, I would like to say that I think the mountain has conceived and brought forth a mouse. The charges which he has made against the government do not amount to very much. I should also like to refer to the hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule). Our friends opposite are willing to swear to the accuracy of. the census of 1891. They say that there were no inaccuracies in connection with them, and the hon. gentleman made the statement
Will the hon. gentleman allow me to say that I made no such statement at all ?

I did not say you did.
I said that hon. gentlemen opposite said so, that they said this upon the other side of the House. However, the hon. member for East Grey said that he knew

My hon. friend (Mr. Holmes) says that it was not the hon. member for East Grey who said that, but it was some other hon. members on this side of the House. Would the hon. gentleman be kind enough to say who it was ?

I alluded to the hon. member for East Grey as referring to his own riding and as stating that the census of 1891 in that riding is much more accurate

than the census of 1901, but I said that hon. members on the other side of the House were willing to swear that the census of 1891 was fairly accurate. However, I happen to have before me the report of the Bureau of Industries of Ontario, in which is given, of course, the results of the census in every municipality, and I find, that, taking the Dominion census of 1901 and comparing it with the municipal census of the same year, and taking the Dominion census of 1891 and comparing It with the municipal census of that year, the last census is much more accurate than the previous one. For instance in the township of Glenelg, in Grey county, I find the difference between the municipal census of 1901 and the Dominion census to be 53, while in 1891, the difference between the local census and the Dominion census is 281. In Osprey, I find the difference in the first instance 44, and in the second instance 133. Do hon. gentleman opposite consider that the census of 1891 was an accurate census when there is such a disparity ? Do they not agree with me that the census of 1901 is much more accurate ? I do not want to weary the House with too many details. The hon. member for Peel is the mover of this resolution, and I propose to devote a little attention to a series of questions which were asked by him in the House some time ago as to the questions asked by the enumerators and the information returned in connection with the present census. One of the hon. members on the other side of the House, in the course of this discussion, has stated that the cost of the census of 1901 is double that of the census of 1891 for the same work. This has been contradicted time and again, and merely to show that our contention is the correct one, I will quote a few figures for the benefit of the hon. member for Peel. The hon. member for Peel asked certain questions in the House in reference to the questions that were asked in Cardwell, Halton and Peel. In 1891 the number of questions asked in Cardwell, as far as population is concerned, was 384,000, in round numbers, in 1901, 444,000; Halton, 1891, 549,000, 1901. 664,000; Peel, 1891, 386,000, 1901, 465,000. In the matter of agriculture, taking real estate, orchard products, nurseries, vineyards and market-gardens, the number of questions asked in Cardwell in 1891 was 66,000, in 1901. 88,000; Halton in 1891, 96,000, in 1901, 111,000; Peel in 1891, 70,000, in 1901, 71,000; the total number of questions asked in the three counties in 1891 was 1,320,000, while in 1901 it was 1,500,000. The number of questions was much greater in 1901 than in 1891, and this is conclusive evidence of the number of questions asked. Continual reference has been made to the accuracy of the census of 1901. The hon. minister dwelt upon the desirability of having accurate statistics in the census. In order to show that the census of 1891 was
not as accurately taken as it should be let me call the attention of the House to one or two points.
For example, in 1891, the area of land in crops as published in the second volume of the census (Table XYI) was ascertained, not by addition of areas under crops as recorded in the schedule, but by an abstracting process which consisted in taking from the area of improved land the areas of land in forest, in pasture and in orchard and garden-the remainder being land in crops. The total area of the land under crops is in this way shown by volume II of the census, to be 19,904,826 acres; but when the area is reckoned up by the details of crops as given in volume IV (published in 1897) it is found to be only 16,139,295 acres, which is 3,765,531 acres less than the area shown in volume II. The excess in the maritime provinces is 627,522 acres, in Quebec, 966,894 acres; in Ontario, 2,233,957 acres; and in the Northwest Territories, 4,421 acres; but in Manitoba there is a deficiency of 2,270 acres and in British Columbia 64,993 acres. Our friends opposite are convicted out of their own mouths as to the inaccuracies in the census of 1891, and I only give these facts in order to show that while they charge that the present census is inaccurate and unreliable, there is no doubt at all that the census of 1891 in which they place so much confidence is without question inaccurate. In order to show the difference in the number of questions, I may point out that in the census of 1891 there were only 216 questions asked, While in the census of 1901 there were over 600 questions asked or nearly three times a s many. I have under my hand here the schedule relating to farm values upon which there are a series of twenty-seven questions. A good many of these questions involve considerable labour in getting information with respect to them, and that schedule was not used at all in the census of 1891. The department showed* its wisdom in taking these statistics in connection with the last census, because I need hardly point out that information as regards our agricultural standing amongst the nations of the world, is of very great importance indeed to the community. It is apparent on the face of it, that a great deal more work was required from the enumerators in 1901 than from the enumerators in 1891, and that additional work is a complete explanation for the extra cost. If gentlemen on the other side of the House have no greater grievance against the government than they have charged in this campaign, or, than they have charged in this House to-day in connection with the census; then the Liberal party has nothing to fear when they appeal to the electors of Canada. I am satisfied that when the intelligent electors of the Dominion look at the importance of the census of 1901, and its superiority over the census of 1891, they will conceive that the additional money has been spent wisely and well. I may say in

conclusion sir, that the Liberals are quite willing to go to the people of the country on this issue, as on any other issue which has been raised by the Conservative party.
