Mr. Speaker, I do not purpose at this late stage of the session detaining the House very long, but I feel that it is my duty to make some comparisons of the expenditure of the census of 1901 as compared with that of 1891. Before recess the hon. member for Brant (Mr. Heyd) was reading from a newspaper which he claimed had made some erroneous statements and had misrepresented the expenditures of the government in this matter. I was somewhat amused when listening to him reading from that paper ; I thought that the man who printed that paper was putting himself in the position of the boy who would tell a lie although the truth would serve a great deal better. My own opinion is that there was enough that could be truthfully said in criticism of this expenditure without resorting to any false statement. Like any other business men we on this side of the House would not expect that the census of 1901 would be taken as cheaply as that of ten years ago. We all know that new parts of the country have been settled, tbit there are difficulties in taking the census in certain localities that would entail more expense than was required ten years ago. Some progress has been made by the country. When listening to the statement of the lion. Minister of Agriculture (Hon. Mr. Fisher) 1 did think that he had a bad case. Notwithstanding his ability to handle such a question the only excuse that he could advance for this enormous expenditure, compared with the expenditure under the Conservative rule, was that the cost of living had increased. It has been argued by the hon. member for Huron that the extra expenditure would be accounted for by the fact that there were more questions to answer, and that there were one-third more questions to answer, and that therefore it should cost one-third more money. I do not agree with that ; I should think that in taking a census the most difficult and tedious part would be getting from house to house, as we have to-day very large farms and a good deal of time is lost in this way. However, for argument sake we will allow that it is good logic to say that because there are one-third more questions to answer we should except an expenditure one-third larger. That and the argument advanced by the hon. minister as to the additional cost of living are the only tw arguments that have been put forth to justify the fact that this census cost twice as much as the other. I will take for illustration my own riding of North
Middlesex. In 1891 East Middlesex had a population of 25,509 aud the cost of taking the census in that year was $1,646.85. In 1901 we had a population of 26,609 and the cost of taking the census was $3,380.09. You will notice that there Is ah increase in population of 1,040, but it w'ould not be fair to assume that that would be sufficient to offset the additional cost entailed by the one-third extra questions. That being the case the only argument that is left is that of the increased cost of living which my hon. friend from Halton (air. Henderson) has exploded fairly well. But the difference in the cost of the two in this census riding is $1,733.24. As the hon. gentlemen from Brant and from Huron have failed to advance any argument to justify this fact it will be necessary to put forward some one else, and they may have to call on the hon. member from North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton) who could possibly advance the best excuse in defence of this expenditure. Allowing that there are one-third more questions to answer and that this should entail an expense one-third greater, and allowing the extra cost of living, on which the Minister of Agriculture has based his argument, there is still a discrepancy which, as I have said, the hon. member for North Norfolk might be able to explain, but I do think he will have a difficult task. We have in North Middlesex a number of independent men. Trior to the election of 1896 the hon. gentleman who leads the House and his colleagues went up and down this country decrying the Conservative party and declaring that an expenditure of $38,000,000 was bleeding the people white, and that Canada could not stand it. So much was said about this expenditure that the people in my riding really came to the conclusion that there must be something wrong with the Conservative party, and in the election of 1896 they returned a supporter of the government. But, Sir, what did they find ? As soon as the present government got into power it was found that none of the pledges which the people conscientiously believed would be carried were carried out, and they found that the expenditure was not $38,000,000 alone, but it went up and up and up, and the result was that when they came to cast their ballots again in 1900 they sent your humble servant to represent them. That I think is sufficient evidence to show that you cannot hoodwink the people of North Middlesex, so I think that we must have a better explanation of what has become of that extra amount of money that has been expended.
Then let us look at South Middlesex. In 1891 South Middlesex had a population of 18,806, and the cost of the census under Conservative rule was $1,389.53. In 1901 South Middlesex had a population of 18,803, practically the same population, a difference of only three ; but what was the cost of the census under Reform economy ? It was $2,982.84, or in other words

$203.78 more than double what it cost under Conservative rule. I do think that this is a state of affairs which requires some explanation ; and although the hon. member is not in his place to-night some other hon. minister, I hope, will get up and explain how the expense came to be so heavy in this instance. I notice that the arguments have been chiefly of a rather lame Character, and I should like to have some hon. member on the opposite side get up and endeavour to make some kind of a frank explanation. When looking into the Auditor General's Report, I did expect some explanation from the hon. the Minister of Agriculture, to account for this Increase of $1,593.31, or more than double what the taking of the census cost in the particular riding under Conservative rule, other than the extra cost of living. I have no doubt that the cost of taking the census was big enough under Conservative rule, but it has been doubled by hon. gentlemen opposite. Next I come to North Middlesex, which, in 1891 had a population of 19,090. Under Conservative rule the census there cost $1,299.92, whereas in 1901, when the population was 17,455, it cost $2,428.55. In other words, there was a decrease in population of 1,535, and an increase of expenditure of $1,128.63, or almost double that under Conservative rule. That certainly demands explanation. Then in West Middlesex, which in 1891 had a population of 17,28S, the cost under Conservative rule was $1,302.31 ; and in 1901. when it had a population of 15,843, the cost under the Reform regime was $3,113.37, being a decrease in population of 1.445 and an increase in expenditure of $1,811.06. In other words, the cost was more than double under the present regime what it was under Conservative rule. No doubt the majority of us in this House are men who had a good deal of experience in municipal life, and I ask those hon. gentlemen how long would they expect to be returned by the different municipalities if, once they got into office, they were to raise the salaries and increase the expenditure more than double and have nothing more to show for the increase except the rise in the cost of living ? How many hon. gentlemen have known of an assessor in a rural municipality, whose salary has gone up in the last ten years 20 pen cent ? I do not know of any such case. How many directors of insurance companies are there whose salaries have been increased, or school teachers or other men in public employ ? I do not know of any increases corresponding to those in the taking of the census. I do not intend to take up much more time, but I have here the figures from South Huron, the riding in which I now live. The cost of taking the census in South Huron, under Conservative rule in 1891. when it had a population of 19,144, was $1,255.59, and in 1901, when it had a population of 17,448, the cost was $2,090.41. So that there was a decrease in Mr. SHERRITT.
population of 1,696-an increase in the expenditure of $838.82. I think that hon. gentlemen opposite will find it hard to justify that increased expenditure in the county of South Huron. In that county the people are getting a little awake to the condition of things, for they have had the extravagance of this government brought home pretty closely to them in the matter of the dock as well as in the taking of the census. I have no doubt that they will insist on more satisfactory explanation than that we have had here before they will condone these items of expenditure by a party which they have looked upon so long as the champions of economy, working in the interests of the country. I think it is due to some of the members belonging to rural municipalities to offer some explanation on these particular items, and I have not selected any particular counties. I took the ones that first caught my eye, and I find by the statements of. other gentlemen that in the other counties we have a similar record. We should have something else to justify this extravagance besides the increase in the cost of living. Some time ago the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Blain) asked why there was no record of summer fallowing in the census records, and the Minister of Agriculture replied that that was a thing of the past. Surely he could not have been sincere in such a statement ? I must say that in our part of the country the farmer who does not summer-fallow is not considered up-to-date.

This question of
the census, Mr. Speaker, has naturally attracted particular attention, both because it has proved very expensive and because a great many opinions have been expressed reflecting on its accuracy. The public have certainly not that confidence in its results which the Minister of Agriculture has sought to prove to exist. In the first place, as to the cost of the census, it has been very much larger than that of any previous census in Canada. I find that, according to the resolution submitted, the census of 1881 cost $450,000, that of 1891 almost exactly $550,000, and that of 1901, though not yet completed, $1,200,000. How much more work is to be done upon it, of course, the House cannot learn at this time. The fact remains that the last two censuses, those of 1881 and 1891, together cost $1,000,000 completed, and the census of 1901 has cost $200,000 more than the two censuses that preceded it, and it is not yet completed. It will be clear at once to any one who looks at the census returns that the increase in the population does not account for this increase of cost. The population of Canada has increased at the rate of about 10 per cent for each decade. Therefore. while the increased cost of the census of 1891 over that of 1881 was just about in agreement witli the increase of population, that is, about 10 per cent,-it really was 20

per cent more. In the case of this last census, where there was an increase of 10 per cent in the population-there has been an increase in the cost, of considerably over 100 per cent. Now, it is natural, it is inevitable, that the members of this House and the people of this country would seelf to learn why the census has cost so much. The Minister of Agriculture has set up a plea that is not, in one respect, an unfair one-that the census has cost more because it is necessary to pay more to employees now than before. He has argued that the cost of living has increased in Canada to such an extent as to account for the increased remuneration, and I presume that the concluding part of his argument would be that this would account for the enormous increase in the cost of the census. As the increase in the cost of the census has been over 100 per cent, if the hon. minister is right in his argument, the cost of living must have increased over 100 per cent in Canada. If that were precisely correct, I suppose we should find an increase of 100 per cent in the wage or remuneration paid to employees by persons, corporations and governments over what was paid ten years ago. But, as a matter of fact, even with the employees of the government themselves, there is nothing to show that those outside the census bureau are receiving 100 per cent higher salaries than they did ten years ago. If it be true that in the Census Bureau they are receiving 100 per cent increase that Bureau must be the envy of all the departments in Ottawa. I know that the men employed on railways in Canada are receiving 15 or 20 per cent more than they were receiving in 1891. I think the employees of the post office are not receiving, in many cases, any more than they were in 1891. Of course, it must be remembered that, in some cases, these employees are complaining that they are not paid enough. But the government of which the hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Fisher) is a member, for many years did not act at all upon this principle that we should give increases of remuneration to employees of the government. He, with the others, is responsible for the fact that for many years they persisted in refusing to give the civil servants even the statutory increases which, I think, might be properly looked upon as part of the salaries of those officers. So, it seems to me, the minister will need , to suggest to the House some better argument than the increased cost of living and the increase of salary that is being paid, and justly being paid, by the departments of the government to civil servants, in order to account for the increased cost of the census which we are now considering. That argument, to a certain extent, is an ingenious one ; I think that even on a cursory examination it will be found to break down completely.
Now, it is very evident that, while the Minister of Agriculture has some ground
for saying that there is an increase in the wage rate being paid for work in Canada, and that he could not get enumerators to work for tile department if he did not give an increased wage rate, yet, taking the figures, he fails to account for the increased cost by developing that idea and showing that he had paid more for the enumerators. 1 took down the figures given by the hon. gentleman as to the cost of enumerators. Those figures show that the enumeration in 1891 cost $682,000, while that for 1901 cost $878,000. Of course, there must be some mistake, because the whole cost of the census for 1891 was only $549,000. I must have taken the figures down wrongly or the minister must have read them incorrectly from his notes. It is not necessary to labour the point. There is evidently some discrepancy. The great increase in the cost of the census is, to a certain extent, accounted for by the increased number of the enumerators employed. That would come about in this way : It is true that two men ought to do in half the time what one man did before. But if the government pays, and pays so liberally as I think we can show they did, for the time occupied in instructing the enumerators-fairly enough-every additional enumerator would add to the cost of the census. If gentlemen are paid $2 or $3 a day during the time they are receiving instruction, and the number in 1901 is double the number in 1891, that portion of the cost will be doubled. It is not hard to show that the cost of instructing the enumerators has been very considerable. I think it has been unjustifiably large. We find, from the testimony given before the committee of this House, that enumerators who came to meet the commissioner of their census districts were allowed $3 a day during the time they were receiving instruction from the commissioner. Moreover the'y were allowed their expenses, though the testimony given may show that they were at' home at the very time they were receiving instructions. They received $3 a day though the sworn testimony of an officer of the government shows that in some cases they spent only one hour on some of the days they were receiving instructions. So, a man running away from his office or the factory in which he was employed to meet the commissioner appointed by this generous, large-hearted, large-souled administration, received for his well-spent time of one hour, $3 as remuneration and $1.50 or $2 for ' expenses.' Now. if you multiply that by the 8,888 enumerators who were employed by the government in making up this census, I think it will be seen that I have got at a very much more satisfactory reason to account for the enormous increase in the cost of the census than the suggestion'made by the Minister of Agriculture that it is owing to the increased cost of living in Canada, or to any increased rate paid to the enumerators for doing their work.
But not only are the enumerators paid

very handsomely, paid for almost nothing, but in some cases in which they failed to receive a sufficient amount of information in the course of the days spent in the company of the commissioner and were unable to do their work at a later period, they were allowed to visit the commissioner at his home or in the neighbourhood; and these gentlemen who had been paid at the rate of $4 or $5 for one hour on the days on which the commissioner was giving the enumerators information, were paid at the same rate with expenses at an enormous advance over the actual cost, for attending the commissioned again at his home. So that it is quite easy to see that this practice of allowing unreasonable prices, unreasonable remuneration, to the enumerators during the period in which they were receiving their instructions, would account for a great part of the cost of this census. Now, who is responsible for this increase ? Clearly I think the Minister of Agriculture must be held to be entirely responsible. The Minister of Agriculture had ample time in which to prepare his work, he had ample time in which to arrange all these details, he had ample time in which to provide for everything that might transpire ; and if the result goes to show that the Minister of Agriculture, or the gentleman to whom he entrusted this work, did not anticipate all possible sources of loss, all possible chances of increasing unduly the cost of this census, then clearly, to my mind, the Minister of Agriculture must devise some far better defence than suggesting flaws in the preceding census before the people of Canada will acquit him of responsibility for the unduly increased cost of the census of 1901.
But the enumerators are not the only persons who have been paid very liberally. We have it on the sworn testimony of an official of the government that a commissioner who was a particularly favoured gentleman-I do not know that all the commissioners who were employed in taking the census were equally favoured-but we know that in the case of one gentleman at least he was allowed to make an addition of $50 to the bill of costs which he prepared to submit to the department, and that account was passed. There was no audit in the case at all of a satisfactory character, and there was no warrant, no justification, for the increased expenditure. After, the commissioner in question had charged for every day upon which he had been employed, even in writing a letter, or sending a telegraphic message, or receiving a parcel, it could only be shown that he had been employed some fifty days. But he was a generous man, and he added fifty per cent to the fifty days and charged the government for seventy-five days. He made up his bill, and having made it up, on subsequent consultation with some other commissioners appointed by the government, he discovered that he had failed to realize all the advantages Mr. BELL.
that might be derived from his position. He realized that he was far in the rear of what had been attained by some others of his brother commissioners, and he coolly added to that bill $50 more. He charges in the first pl8.ce for every hall he had occupied, he charges for every moment of horse-hire, and he deliberately adds a lump sum to this bill later on. Charges for hall rent, for horse-hire, and for stationery, by which he adds something like $50 to that which was already a most liberal bill, and the whole amount is paid.
Now, if the people of Canada want to find out how the census has cost so much, all they have to do is to take the few occasions in which it has been possible to get at these accounts, and they will see why this census has cost so much. It is simply because the only limit to the size of the bills rendered by the commissioners and paid by the government, was the idea of what the government would stand on the part of the commissioners. The measure of the bite was the appetite of the man, and there is no evidence to show that in any case was there any restriction or control exercised, but throughout all the census accounts, so far as they can be understood by a cursory glance, and particularly so far as they can be better understood in view of the evidence taken before the committee, the man asked and received what he pleased. That accounts very easily for the enormously increased cost of the census, and it goes to show that the government did not exercise any particular control. They certainly started off in the most liberal fashion; they increased the cost of taking the census by their own act, in the first place, by advancing the remuneration from' three cents per name to five cents per name; from fifteen cents per farm to twenty-five cents per farm; from twenty cents per factory to thirty cents per factory. There is an increase all round averaging over fifty per cent; and still, in addition to these enormous charges, all the accounts throughout. in the eyes of men who were familar with the locality and with the circumstances, go to show that after being paid these enormously high rates, the enumerators and1 the commissioners as well, were allowed to make irregular additions to their bills and these bills were honoured.
Now, a good part of the census commissioners may not have been quite as highly favoured as was the gentleman whose conduct was investigated before the committee. The facts were brought out that he was already an official of the government, employed, but I do not think very busily employed, in a different class of work altogether under different departments. In the case of Mr. Hurley, of Bast Hastings, it is seen that during the period in which he was engaged in taking the census he drew from his work under the Fishery Department, $441, and for his work under the census commissioner, $330 more, or a total

payment of ?771. Now, why was this gentleman favoured so much ? I suppose the reason was that he was a defeated candidate. He had been a candidate at the preceding election, and although defeated by tbe people, not only is the whole patronage of his riding placed in bis hands, but he is also appointed to supervise the officials of the provincial government in connection with the fisheries, and on top of that he is appointed a census commissioner, and above all he is allowed to pass accounts of the liberal character described, in which he is paying a man $3 a day for one hour's attendance, and is allowed to add fifty per cent to the lump sum claimed on his own account, and the whole thing is paid by the government. Under these circumstances, if it is necessary for the minister to raise the *question of inorelased cost, of increased remuneration, of increased wages, the whole thing is, it seems to me, quite clear, it is an occasion in which the spoils system was in full operation. No man need apply for a position who was not a good staunch party supporter, and having become a good staunch party supporter, he could depend upon getting the most favoured nation treatment when he came to do business with the government. There was no question whatever as to his account-simply present it and have it paid.
I find in my own county, the county of Pictou, in one comparatively small polling section, a compact section in which the houses are all along the main roads, one man is allowed twenty-four and a half days horse-bire for taking the farms in that one polling section. There were no factories, simply a farm settlement. Well, I would think it a very pleasant pastime to visit on foot every house in that polling section in two or three days; still a man is allowed to get twenty-four days and horse-hire.
Now, the criticism which has been addressed by this side of the House generally against the census, has been to the effect that it has been enormously costly, unreasonably costly; and, in the second1 place, we are inclined to believe that it will prove to be not only a very costly census, but when the whole matter is completed and all the .accounts are closed, it will be found to be not a very satisfactory census. In reply to that the minister goes on to show that there were some errors in the census of 1891. He says that in some cases in 1891 the enumerators' schedules were not very carefully made out. He refers in particular to the schedules in connection with the fisheries, which he says were not available and which were not produced by the compilers. That may be. A further statement of the bon. Minister of Agriculture is that in some cases in 1891 exceptions were made by tlie commissioners in favour of the enumerators. That may be. The hon. minister rend a list in which he said that in North and South Waterloo, Frontenac. East Sim-coe and elsewhere, the commissioners, or
managers, in 1891 departed from their rule of paying three cents per name and allowed $3 per day. It struck me while listening to that statement that in most cases where this had occurred, the sections were comparatively small, and the probability was that it was impossible to get any men to do the work of enumerating the census in these districts for three cents a name. It was likely that the population was so small that it was necessary to make some concessions. But admitting that there were irregularities in 1891, that simply increases our surprise at, or perhaps our admiration of, the fact that in the case of the census of 1901 the Minister of Agriculture is enabled to distance the performances of the bureau in 1891 by over 100 per cent. But admitting that there was a possibility of some irregularity in that case, we are led to believe, from the very statement made by the hon. minister, that there must be some enormous irregularities connected with the census of 1891. There is one difficulty about the form of criticism that the hon. gentleman has employed. It will be remembered that last year this same matter was brought up in the House in connection with the discussion on the budget, and a great many different parcels of census returns were laid upon the Table. It was charged that irregularities had occurred, and in fact it was insinuated that worse than irregularities had occurred. It was practically stated that the census of 1891 was padded. The impropriety of introducing any such evidence into this House lay in the fact that it was an ex-parte statement. It was a statement made by the parties who had possession of all the documents, which were withheld from those who were opposed to them, and there was no possibility for those thus opposed availing themselves of that evidence. The hon. Minister of Agriculture has referred to some persons in different counties in Quebec, a lot of schedules to have them examined there by persons who were friendly to the census of 1901 and hostile to the census of 1891. This was giving an unfair advantage, and there could be no satisfactory outcome from such a decision unless the government were prepared to grant our request that there should be a full inquiry made into the position of tbe census of 1891 and the census of 1901 by some disinterested and competent party.
They would not allow the Public Accounts Committee to see the schedules, but they would cart them all over the country for others to examine.

That being the case, it is very clear that the hon. Minister of Agriculture cannot expect 1o secure the assent of this House to the course which he has followed. He cannot expect to bring conviction to the mind of any hon. member on this side of the House by the criticism to which he has resorted. ' It is very evident from the

defence which the hon. minister has put up that he has devoted a certain portion of the staff which is employed by him in the census staff not to the work of making the census of 1901 as perfect and complete as possible, but to the work of criticising, examining and seeking to find flaws in a census that is ten years old.
Trying to discredit it.

Trying to discredit the census of 189.1. That is the work to which the officers of the census bureau have been devoted, and it is not so hard to understand! how a considerable addition has been made to the cost of the census of 1901. Not only has the hon. Minister of Agriculture engaged in taking a census, but, recognizing tiie fact that his census does not have the confidence of the people of Canada, recognizing the fact that it has been exposed to a great deal of hostile criticism, and realizing that he must make some defence, it is very clear that a great deal of industry has been devoted, not to perfecting the census of 1901, but to an endeavour to make it appear better by pointing out defects in the one that precede(Tit. That would be a perfectly fair and legitimate comparison if it could be made from both sides. If the friends of the census of 1891 were in the position to join the hon. minister in the investigation and compare these two censuses. If we were in a position to go and see what was good and1 what bad gnd to judge for ourselves, then it would be perfectly fair, but the hon. minister comes forward and produces this evidence which has been collected by him, but which-and I do not assume that he has not been perfectly honest in the matter, or that he is making statements that he does not believe true- is entirely ex-parte. He is simply playing the game with loaded dice, and he cannot expect that any such defence as he is making is going to satisfy the House or the country as to the_ merits of the census of 1901. The hon. minister has said a good deal about the comparative time in which the work of compilation and enumeration has been completed. He has drawn a great many comparisons very much to the advantage of the census of 1901 and very much to the disadvantage of the census of 1891. This all comes under the same category as that to which I have referred. We must leave these matters for full and satisfactory consideration until the time has arrived when the two censuses have been completed and can be compared as completed. It is impossible to judge them any sooner than that. If the hon. minister has succeeded in having a perfectly satisfactory census made in 1901, we will be glad to know it when we have had time to study it fully. At this moment, after two and a half years have elapsed, only the first volume of the census has been published, and the schedules which relate to the industries of Canada, and the schedules for which the hon. minister claims 1

a great deal of credit as having been taken in addition to those prepared in 1891, have not been compiled or submitted to this parliament, and we are not in a position to judge of the advantages of the census in that respect. It appears from the claim made by the hon. minister that a great many more questions were asked in the census of 1901 than in the census of 1891. That is, I suppose, up to a certain point, in the right direction, but, when the census bureau undertakes to collect more information than can be reduced within a reasonable time into tabulated form, it is submitting the country to an expenditure from which the country is not likely to derive any substantial benefit whatever. Although the questions in the schedules have been increased from 216 in 1891 to 561 in 1901, the fact apparently remains that we have not at this moment derived any more advantage whatever from this large number of additional questions, because they have not been compiled, and if the answers are permitted to remain in the forms of schedules uncompleted and uncompiled and inaccessible to the public, of what value is this large number of questions ? It would have been better far for the country, if the government had been satisfied with a smaller number of questions, and if they had collected the information in such a manner as to enable them to have it in tabulated form at the earliest possible moment. We are at a disadvantage in not having the two censuses completed, because we cannot compare them. I was rather amused at the criticism of my hon. friend from South Brant (Mr. Heyd), who apparently found a great deal to excite his criticism in the fact that the census-takers of 1891 had devoted a good deal of time to ascertaining how many rooms were in the homes which were occupied by the people of Canada, and particularly when he came to tell the House about the statistics relating to those who only occupied one room, he seemed to look upon that as the most idle and improvident, and ridiculous thing that could be imagined. The idea of spending time over these poor people who could only afford to live in one room. Was that the idea he had in his mind ?
No.

Then, I would like to know what was in that great mind possibly like the judge who shook his head, there was nothing in it. There is nothing more important in the census forms, as a portrayal of the condition of the country than a return showing how many families have to live in one room. There is uo greater indication of the need of social reform, and occasionally of governmental and municipal interference, than that anything like a large percentage of the people of the country should have to live in one room. There is nothing that marks more distinctly the progress of the people and their advancement, than that the number who live in one room is diminish-

ing. There is perhaps no feature in that census to which the reformer of a future day, who is trying to get an idea of what Canada was in 1891, would attach more importance than to that very statement. He would want to know how many of the people of Canada were obliged to live in such a poor condition, that they were compelled to live in a dwelling of one room. These facts relating to our population, are to my mind of high importance. They give us a picture of our country as it is ; they show what the requirements of our country are at a given date, and they measure the progress of the people more correctly even, than the statistics relating to the creation of wealth and its development In industrial pursuits. I cannot understand why my hon. friend from Brant (Mr. Heyd) should criticise the census of 1891 on the ground that it had devoted a great deal of attention to the humbler classes of the people. It seems to me that a census could not he better employed, than in that very work. We have the fact remaining then, that the census of 1901 has been an enormously expensive census ; that it has cost us at least $500,000 more than it should have cost, and so far as I can judge, there is no prospect of its being completed within the very near future. An enormous part of the figures secured by the enumerators have not been compiled yet, and judging by the amount of money voted this year, it is not unreasonable to say that it looks as though that census would never be completed. I believe that when two or three years have passed, and we have ascertained more closely what the census of 1901 have brought forth, we will be able to say that it has not only been a most costly census, but a most defective one as well. My hon. friend (Mr. Heyd) treated with a great deal of scorn, certain criticisms which he found in a broad sheet, on the compilation of this census in the department. The hon. gentleman ought not to be too quick to pledge his word and his standing in this House, in the positive assertion that these statements are absolutely unfounded. He may have to swallow a good many of these statements before he is much older. So far, it has not been possible to secure evidence on some of these points. But the day is not far distant when evidence will be secured.
Why make the statement before you secure evidence ?
You would never make any statement if you followed that rule.
The time will come when these statements will be verified.
There are three deliberate statements made in that sheet, which on the authority of the census commissioner are absolutely untrue. What are you going to do about it ?
We are going to prove it.
Go on and prove it. I would rather take the word of the census commissioner.

We know, although we cannot prove it to a demonstration yet, that the schedules, in the Census Department have been changed ; that in some cases figures have been altered by the compilers ; that the returns as compiled are not the returns as received in the census office from the enumerators ; that the census compilers have corrected what they thought to be errors, and in some cases they committed errors in altering what was actually correct. I do not know exactly to what extent this has gone. We did not know until recently to what extent the government had gone in allowing enumerators and commissioners to pay themselves. We only succeeded in getting one or two witnesses before the committee but so far as it went, I never heard of any lead or vein that seem to give better promise of great returns, if it could be worked out. There can be no doubt that it will be worked out. The manner in which the government have tried to discredit the census taken ten years ago ; the manner in which they have done it in the dark to a certain extent; the manner in which they have made use of their position to take census documents out of the custody of the department and to distribute them in the hands of partisans in order to discredit the census of ten years ago, is a sufficient warrant that the moment the opportunity arises a complete investigation into the census of 1901 will have to be made in order to satisfy the people of the country. The cost of this census, let it be borne in mind, is not paid by the members of this House alone, but by the people of Canada, and if the census is not satisfactory, the people of the country will demand an investigation. They will want to understand how it is possible, that whereas the census of 1891 contained a large number of questions in excess of those asked in 1881, it entailed a comparatively small increase of cost. They will want to know how it is that the census of 1901, containing in the same way an increased number of questions no man can possibly account for the increased cost. A large number of these questions apply only to those engaged in certain trades and avocations, like the fishermen, and the enumerators are not required to visit every man in the country in order to get these questions answered. All the factories in Canada are comparatively few, and all the fishermen of Canada are few compared with the whole population. The great cost of enumeration must manifestly be in visiting, individually, the people who are enumerated. You may increase questions by the hundred and not add much to the labour of an enumerator.
The addition of 100 per cent to the number of questions could not possibly, under a fair and honest management, add anything like 100 per cent to the cost. It might

add only a very limited amount to the cost of the census. All these things being taken Into consideration, the fact remains that the census has been enormously costly and there is a grave suspicion on the part of those who looked into it most carefully that it will prove to be an unsatisfactory census. The government refused to employ a man of recognized ability, I might say of eminence, as a statistician ; they passed him over to take into their employment a man whom they selected, simply on the ground of his party allegiance. They passed over a trained statistician, a man who has a continental. a world-wide reputation, and they took an untried man, with the result that might have been expected. Then in regard to the work of enumeration, instead of employing the old enumerators who had had experience. they employed an altogether untrained and inexperienced body of enumerators. No man who was employed in the previous census was employed in this one.
Shame.
My hon. friend says shame. He is pleased with that act and why is he so gratified with the fact that not one of the men employed in 1891 was employed in 1901 ?
We wanted a better quality.

Wanted a better quality ; if the measure of quality has been the cost of the service, then evidently the qualifications were very high. Not one of the old enumerators was employed, no matter how competent he might be, because he was of the wrong party stripe. Members of the House of Commons who are saying to me across the House that this was quite right are simply proclaiming that they took advantage of their position here to make a present to their party supporters throughout Canada of $750,000. on the good and satisfactory ground that they were good party supporters and would vote the Liberal ticket. The result goes to show the people what it costs them to have in power a government that views matters in this way. If the government had taken the experienced census manager whom they had at their call and had employed the experienced census enumerators whom they could have found throughout the country, there can be no doubt that the census would have been better taken and taken at a much reduced cost. I would not have thought it proper on my part to enter into any defence of the Dominion statistician from the charges that were made against him by his minister to-day ; I thought that when the Minister of Agriculture said so positively that the officer who took the census of 1891 had committed such blunders and done such bad work in that census that he would not allow him to take this one, it was no part of mine or of any member on this side of the House to say a word in condemnation of the minister's ac-Mr. BELL.
tion. However, the very errors in the census of 1891 which the minister was using and advancing as the reason why he should not employ the statistician to take this census were discovered by him after the present census had been taken. He could have had no knowledge of these errors up to the time and until long after the time he commenced taking the census of 1901.
The hon. gentleman forgets the errors that were pointed out in this House in 1893 and 1891.
Those were not the errors cited by the hon. minister on this occasion.
They( were quite sufficient.

The only errors pointed out on that occasion were errors not on the part of the head of the census bureau, but on the part of some enumerators, particularly I think of one in the county of King's, N.S.; no charge was made against the head of the statistical department. I think it would be admitted that a very much better and more satisfactory defence will have to be made by the Minister of Agriculture and his supporters before they will convince the people of Canada that this has been a cheap or economical census. And yet we are perfectly willing to be reasonable and fair and wait until time gives us the opportunity to know exactly what the present census is. I think they will require to produce some very valuable volumes and excellent results before they can persuade the people that it is a good and well-taken census. There is one little fact by which we can judge of the comparative merit and ability of the men managing the two censuses; that is the fact that while the first results were given to the people of Canada by the census bureau at about the same length of time after the enumeration in 1891 and 1901, I think in the month of August in each ease, the census department in 1891 gave the population exactly almost, with an error of only 500, less than 600, while in the case of the census taken in 1901, the first returns of population, made about the same period, were in error to the extent of 44,000 ; the error in the census of 1901 was nearly one hundred times as great as that of the census of 1891. We know that. ; we can only guess at what may be revealed by the publication of the later volumes of the census. But we know that so far as the census returns of the population of Canada are concerned, the head of the census bureau in 1891 came within less than 600 of what was found in the end to be the exact population, and that in the present census the error is somewhere in the neighbourhood of 40,000 or 50,000. That is a .simple fact, but it is a test case, and goes to show that there was more accuracy and speed in compiling the returns in 1891 than in 1901, and I will

be agreeably surprised if it does not prove true as to all the succeeding volumes that there Is tbe same measure of inaccuracy to be found in 1901 as compared with the census of 1891, in every other respect as there was evidenced In that first estimate of the population made in the two successive censuses. I think enough has been proved to show that in every part of the census work there has been an enormous increase of cost, and it has not been shown, so far as I can discover-and I am sure I approached the subject with an open mind- that there was any increased efficiency to compensate the country for the increased cost. Therefore it strikes me that Canada has every reason to be dissatisfied with a census whose only merit is that it has put an enormously large sum of money into the hands of the good supporters of the party now in power.

I had no intention, Mr. Speaker, of addressing the House on this subject, and consequently have not followed the example of hon. gentlemen opposite and collected material for a speech, I shall not trespass on your patience to any great extent. The only reason why I do obtrude myself into this debate is because the county which I have the honour to represent has been referred to by the member for North Middlesex (Mr. Sherritt), in such a way that I can hardly afford to allow his remarks to go unchallenged. The hon. gentleman, in comparing the labour of taking the census of 1901 with the work done in 1891, argued that as the population was less in the later period, the work of taking the census must have been correspondingly decreased. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that that does not follow at all.
I find, on looking at the census of 1901, that in some cases over 400 more questions were asked than in the previous census. In the farmers' schedules 127 questions were asked in 1901 as compared with 75 in 1891. In those of the latter are included four questions relating to farm buildings, twelve to classified areas of farm land, twenty-two to orchard trees, vines and fruits, thirty-seven to field crops, twenty-six to live stock and animal products, and twenty-three to values of lands, buildings, field and fruit crops and labour. And no system of agricultural enumeration is satisfactory which does not take account of the areas devoted to agricultural purposes, the schedules are framed to procure as far as practicable the acreage as well as the production of every crop. That shows that the work done in 1901, in this particular item, is over three-quarters more than what was done in 1891. To my mind, that certainly, supposing the cost is more than double, fully justifies that expenditure. I find also that with reference to the forest industry, fifty questions were asked in each case in the census of 1901 as compared with twenty-two in the

volume was published in 1897, so that we on this side have got a few years yet to j wait before we will have reached the length of time taken by bon. gentlemen opposite to complete their census. They are therefore a little premature in saying that our census will never be completed. As regards the total cost of the census, I think any increase in the expenditure is amply justified by the much more complete and accurate information obtained and by the greatly increased work that had to be done at headquarters to compile and collate all that information, and we have the satisfaction of knowing that we have a. census upon which we can rely, and not, as in the case of the last one, a census in which much of the information given was absolutely unreliable. And we have, in addition to that, the fact that the population has increased very much, which, of course, added to the cost as compared with 1891, not only in the enumeration, but in the work of compilation here at Ottawa.
I should at any stage of the session despair of bringing hon. gentlemen to vote for the motion of my hon. friend from Peel-

Hear, hear.
Mr. CLANCY-and I still further despair of convincing my hon. friend who says :
' Hear, hear '-but I especially despair on this occasion of hon. gentlemen opposite doing what is right. I am not going into the discussion of this question generally-

Hear, hear.
Mr. CLANCY-and I am glad to have the approval in advance of my hon. friend from West York (Mr. Campbell). I promise the hon. gentleman I will be only a few minutes.
1 want to deal mainly with one constituency, and 1 choose that of the whip of the Liberal party (Mr. Calvert) certainly a distinguished gentleman to occupy so distinguished a position. I think that constituency would be a fair sample of Liberal morality. It would be an abomination to suppose that there was anything worse in the riding of the whip of the Liberal party in connection with the taking of the census than in any other constituency. That hon. gentleman recommended all the officers and knew all about them, and I say that no one would imagine that any hon. gentleman on the other side of the House could maintain a higher standing with regard to these appointments than the whip of the party. I meed hardly say that every hon. gentleman on the other side who recommended the commissioner in his riding and even went so far as to recommend that every one of the enumerators must be held responsible. Now, the constituency represented by the whip of the Liberal party is West Middlesex. The population of that riding in 1891 was 17,288, and it costs $1,302.21 to take the census that year. In 1901, the riding did not have so large a population.
It will be remembered that the Liberal party

were in opposition during a very considerable part of the decade, and it will be remembered also that they were among the most active immigration agents of .the United States during that period and lost no opportunity of assuring the people that Canada was not a country fit to live in. The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Rt. Hon. Sir Richard Cartwright) made the statement in this House a session or two ago that the London ' Advertiser ' had within that period some 900 subscribers in the United-States, all of whom had left Canada. This kind of thing may account for the population of the riding having shrunk from 17,288 in 1891 to 15,543 in 1901. But what does the House suppose it cost to take the census during this year of lower population ? Instead of $1,302.31, the cost was $3,113.37. Let me give you some instances of Liberal economy. I am not quoting from mere hearsay. We bad an examination into this matter before the Public Accounts Committee and I have before me the evidence taken in that examination. Take the case of the village of Glencoe, a little place of about 1,000 inhabitants. The recording in that village cost $57.40 and the horse-hire was $63. Then, take the little village of Newbury, the population of which is about three or four hundred. The recording there cost $29.50 while the horse-hire in the village cost $27. Then, take the town of Strathroy, the town in which the Liberal whip resides. The recording in the town of Strathroy cost $173.50 and the horse-hire $186. Putting it all together the recording cost $260.15, and the horse-hire $276 of these places. Let me give you some of the evidence. I am sorry that my hon. friend from South Brant (Mr. Heyd) is not in his place. But, as I have said, I shall not give mere hearsay, but shall quote from the evidence given before the Public Accounts Committee. Of course, it will be understood that we have merely touched the fringe when we have investigated West Middlesex. Here is the evidence of Mr. McDougal, the commissioner for the riding :
Q. Do you know Mr. Alex. Leach of Strathrov' A. I do.
Q. What does he do ?
A. I do not know what he does.
Q. Never inquired I suppose. Does he live in the town ?
A. He lives in the town.
Q. How old is he? Seventy?
A. I would Judge that he was probably more, he is a good age, an old gray-haired man.
Q. Is he a delicate man?
A. He is.
My hon. friend from South Brant said they had selected the best men.
Q. Do you think he would be able to walk from house to house to take the census?
A. I could not say, although he is very crippled.
Q. Does he use crutches ?
A. No sir. not that I am aware of.
Q. But would you feel bound to allow him horse-hire on account of his age ?

A. If he put it in his account I certainly would allow it.
Q. Well, you seem to have allowed Mr. Leach twenty-two days' horse-hire ?
A. Yes.
Q. Aggregating $33 ? and you say if he put it in, you would have allowed it to him on account of his age ?
A. Not altogether on that account ; I would have allowed it because he had it in his account.
Q. All you had to do was to find it in his account and you allowed it ?
A. I allowed that part of it.
Q. Is Mr. Duncan Patterson an old gentleman seventy years of age?
A. He is quite an old man.
Q. Does he reside in Strathroy ?
A. I think he does, or very near it on the town line.
Q. What is he-a healthy rugged man ?
A. I would not call him so.
Q. He is able to go about from house to house?
A. I would judge so.
Q. Is he old enough now to elicit your sympathies ?
A. I did not have any sympathies.
Q. You have none. ?
A. No. sir.
Q. If he put in horse-hire, you allowed it because it was in there ?
A. Yes, -sir, because it was in there.
Q. Do you know Mr. John R. Olarke ?
You see, Mr. Speaker, I take them in consecutive order.
A. I do, sir.
Q. How old a man is he ?
A. I could not say, probably more than sixty.
Q. Is he a vigouroUs man ?
A. I would not call him so.
Q. Delicate is he ?-A. Fairly healthy I think, although he has a delicate appearance, but I could not say whether he is delicate or not.
Q. You would think he was able to go about at sixty taking the census in a place like Strathroy?-A. In part of it.
Q. Now he is allowed fourteen days' horse-hire, $21. You allowed the others partly on account of age ?-A. I beg pardon, I did not say so.
Q. Well, because Mr. Clarke was fortunate enough to put it in there ?-A. Yes, sir.
Q. That is the reason ?-A. Yes, sir.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I could read pages of that kind of history in West Middlesex. I shall not detain the House further than to say that Mr. McDougal-and I take It as a fair sample-declares in his evidence that he did not make any declaration nor did he receive any declarations as to the accuracy of his accounts ; all he had to do in every instance was to put in the account and it was paid.
And to vote right.

And to vote right. We have there in evidence that whatever account was put in it was paid, although the law requires that a declaration should be made in every case, the commissioner stated upon oath that he took no declarations, contrary to law, and contrary to a statement made by the Minister of Agriculture who, in his place in this House, when he was defending the cost of the census, declared that in every instance the solemn declaration of
the parties was taken in regard to the matter. Yet we find in that single sample selected, that the commissioner states that in no case did he take any declarations from the parties who had been employed on the census. Now, Mr. Speaker, I think I have said enough to make it perfectly clear that the most wretched conduct prevailed throughout the whole of Canada in the taking of this census, and one evidence Is the fact that the census of 1891 cost $449,991, while that of 1901 cost $1,19S,26S. I have given you a fair sample in the only case which I had occasion to examine, and it was a fair sample of the system that pervaded the whole thing from start to finish. Is it any wonder that this alarming cost should be saddled upon the people of Canada for useless purposes ? Why, Sir, the census in many cases are utterly useless, they are crowded with the most useless tables, and these are given as a reason for having such an enormously increased cost. But you can see the folly at once. These are mere pretexts for that condition of things. I have given you a fair sample of how the accounts have been padded out. It was stated by some gentlemen that the census have been altered. If any hon. gentleman now is prepared to dispute that I will read from the evidence taken before the Public Accounts Committee, that they were altered, that the schedules were changed, that slips were put in, and that this was of general occurrence. There is no use for hon. gentlemen to deny these facts, they are here in evidence and can be produced, and they know it perfectly well. Now I have nothing more to say in conclusion but this
Hear, hear.
Well, I know my hon. friend is impatient. I sympathize with my hon. friend. I am astonished at his moderation, under such circumstances, that he did not say ' hear, hear ' long ago.	,
Read him the evidence.

Well, I will not weary the hon. gentleman, I will not put such a strain upon him. I can only tell Mm that the record of the government in taking this census is a perfectly scandalous one, it is one over which the hon. gentlemen opposite should hang their heads in shame. I shall have much pleasure in supporting the amendment of my hon. friend from Peel (Mr. Blain), and I shall expect that our friends opposite will do the same. If there ever was a motion brought up iu this House that invited the courage of hon. gentlemen, it is the motion of my hon. friend to censure the conduct of the government in making this census. Not only have they cost this enormous sum, but they are of little value in many respects. They were made in some cases by men declared to be so old that they could not walk about the streets, men as stated by my hon. friend from Pictou (Mr. COMMONS
Bell) who were mere voters'and were nearly past the voting age. I repeat that I shall be astonished if hon. gentlemen opposite do not support my hon. friend's motion.

This Mr. Joyce has passed the examination in one optional subject, and is therefore entitled to an increase of $50.
Why is he paid a certain sum for one optional subject ?

Under the Civil Service Act, if one of the clerks passes an examination for a subject which is optional, such as typewriting or stenography, he becomes entitled, not as a matter of course, but in the discretion of the government, to an increase of $50.
To provide for the salary of a second-class clerk, E. P. Drake, notwithstanding anything in the Civil Service Act, $1,200.

The circumstances under which this vote is required are as follows : Mr. Drake is a staff sergeant in the mounted police. He enlisted on the 14tli August, 1888. He has done work in the inside service, and is a very good officer. At the present time he receives $1,131.50, and it is proposed to give him an additional salary, which will raise liis salary to $1,200.
What service is he now in ?
He is In the inside service. He enlisted formerly as a constable and then became a sergeant, after which he was transferred to the inside service at Ottawa. He performs clerical work.
Does he take the place of any other clerk in the inside service, or is he an additional clerk ?

No, he is taking nobody's place. He has been transferred. At the present time he is not permanent. We intend to make him a permanent officer and give him a salary of $1,200. The increase will be the difference between $1,131.50 and $1,200.
Where did he get $1,131 ?
At Ottawa. He has been in Ottawa for seven years.
It is not the appointment of an additional officer at all ?
No.

How far is it permissible to establish a branch like that without any amendment to the law 7 Have you the right to establish all the branches you think it wise to establish without the authority of law, simply making it a departmental matter 7

There is no doubt that with this amount of money voted by parliament the government has perfect authority to create such a work, but it will last only one year. Unless it is provided next year it will lapse, ipso facto; it cannot be continued from year to year as it could if it were established by statute.
I take it that the more proper way would be to establish a branch by statute.

I think it would be preferable to establish it this way. It is experimental and may not prove conclusively satisfactory and therefore I think it better to do it in this way. If it works well perhaps the idea of my .hon. friend will then be adopted but at the present time I think my hon. friend will agree that it is better to have it as it is.
We already have a statistical branch and as this is simply collecting statistics along another line I do not see why this should not be added to the statistical branch.

It is collecting statistics on another line of a very special character, and as it is stated in the memorial I presented to the House it is proposed to issue a volume to be entitled : ' The Mineral Resources of Canada.' I doubt very much if we would have in the Department of Agriculture a staff of' such special knowledge and competence as to collect the information which is to be included in this volume. It will require the services of expert mineralogists to perform this work.
It seems to me it would be the easiest matter in the world to appoint an expert on this subject to the statistical branch.
I do not say my hon. friend may not be right.

It seems to me that if you are to create a sub-department of the Department of the Interior called the mines branch, it would be necessary to have a statute eventually; I think the hon. member for East Grey is perfectly correct about that. I would like to know what Dr. Haanel's position is at present; what are his duties in the Department of the Interior, how long has he been in the department and what have been his duties up to the present time ?

Dr. Haanel has been in the employment of the government as superintendent of mining for three or four years, my impression is four years. He has been performing duties, an account of which will be found in the report of the Minister of the Interior, he has been collecting material, looking after the different interests in mining, looking after the establishment of an assay office in Vancouver and cognate subjects. He has made an annual report of his work.

As far as mining iii my own province is concerned I have not heard of any efforts on his part; it may be that he has done something about the assay office at Vancouver. My hon. friend's description of his duties seems to be rather vague; the mere fact that he is superintendent of mining does not convey much information unless we know his duties and what he has accomplished. Has he superin-431*
tended the construction of the assay office or what has he done in connection with it V

He established the assay office, bought the machinery, had charge of the work of construction and has carried on everything in regard to the establishment of the office. I am sorry to say that I am not as familiar with his report as 1 might be.
Mr. LaRIVIERE. I quite understand that it is very hard to become familiar with the work of the assay office at Vancouver. I tried to gain admission to it, and although I disclosed my identity as a member of this House I was refused admission.

Mr. LaRIVIERE. I do not know that there should be any such regulations.

He has full charge of it and superintends its management. The duties of Dr. Haanel are certainly; more important than my hon. friends opposite are disposed to believe. The mining development of this country is increasing very fast and Dr. Haanel, as I am informed, is very often communicated with by people from all parts of the country to examine samples and mines, and his labours I understand, have been of great value and assistance.

I am not finding fault with his labours; I am trying to find out what he really has done, and I realize that my right hon. friend is not familiar with the department as the Minister of the Interior would be, but he has the information at his hand and possibly we can succeed in getting at something. I have not heard anything that this gentleman has done in my province, but he may have done a great deal somewhere else, and I would like to know what it is. Will my right hon. friend tell us what the qualifications of Dr. Haanel are for the work ?

He was at first professor in the University of Victoria at Cobourg and then at Syracuse, N.Y. The report of Dr. Haanel will be found on page 17 of the Sessional Papers of 1902, No. 25.

If I remember correctly, the office established was that of superintendent of the mines, which has no connection with this.

I am informed by my deputy that Mr. Pearce was for many years superintendent of mines. It is not a new office. Mr. Pearce, who has a very wide range of knowledge of the geology of the territories, has been made chief inspector of the surveys there, and Dr. Haanel was appointed in his place.

I know Mr. Pearce very well and he appears to be a sort of itinerant in his duties, as he has held many offices. He has now assumed the dignity of head of a branch office, and no doubt he will soon be surrounded by a dozen clerks.
Mi-. BORDEN (Halifax). It seems to me that the head of a branch of this kind should have practical knowledge. I would ask my right hon. friend what practical experience or training Dr. Haanel has had 1

My recollection of Dr. Haanel is that he is a distinguished graduate of a university in Germany and was professor of mineralogy and geology in Victoria University, when that university became affiliated with Toronto University, it ceased to maintain the chair of mineralogy and geology, and in that way it lost the services of Db. Haanel. I have heard the late Chancellor Nellis of Victoria University speak in the highest terms of Professor Haanel.

1 do not know anything thing about Dr. Haanel. I do not think I have ever heard of him before, and that was why I was anxious to find out what were his qualifications to preside over this mines branch. What you require in that position is a man that has not only theoretical but practical knowledge, and a man, in the prime of life at least, and I would prefer a young man. We should not be satisfied with selecting some gentleman who has occupied a theoretical chair at'some university, but who would not be likely to give the practical service which a branch of tin's kind demands. If we are to spend money for this very important service, it is, of course, desirable, as my right hon. friend will recognize, that we should have the very best man we can procure at the head of it. office. But it is our duty to find out something about him as this vote contemplates a very important addition to the service, and that is the reason why I think we should have a little more knowledge as to his qualifications than has been given to us this evening.

I am obliged to my hon. friend the Postmaster General (Hon. Sir William Mulock) for giving information which I had not myself. I know Dr. Haanel, having met him once or twice. My hon. friend (Mr. Sproule) knows that in the Railway Department and in the Public Works Department there are officers, engineers especially, who have been in the department

Mr. Low was formerly attached to the Geological Survey, and resigned some years ago. I have here the Civil Service Act, and I am inclined to think that the First Minister puts a strained interpretation on it. It says that the ' Civil Service Act shall include and consist of all classes of employees in or under the several branches of the executive government and in the office of the Auditor General,' and included in subsections. A and B. Subsection A mentions deputy heads and officers who have special qualifications, including in that term, I suppose, draughtsmen and civil engineers. But I understood the right hou. gentleman to say that half the men employed in the public works do not coine under the Civil Service Act.

They can come under it, undoubtedly, but what I had in rny mind was the regular service, in which all the officers are admitted to the responsibilities and advantages of the Act, participating for instance in the retirement fund. I repeat that there are many officers, engineers, in the Public Works Department and in the Railways Department, who do not contribute to the pension fund, and who properly do not come under the terms of the Civil Service Act. A good many do, but quite a number do not.

They come under it so far as promotion and salaries go, though they do not participate in the retirement allowance. But as I always understood the Act, it does not say they ' may.' It says that all classes of the employees in the government of Canada or in the office of the Auditor General, appointed by Order in Council, ' shall ' come under it. Schedule A mentions the deputy heads and officers who have special technical qualifications, chief clerks, first, second and third-class clerks, and messengers. Then, going on, schedule B mentions the officers in the Customs and Inland Revenue. I always understood that not only they must come under it, but all the promotions must be made under the Act.
The PRIME MINISTER, No, the Civil Service Act, as my hon. friend knows, is full of mysteries, and for my part I have never had time to undertake to master it. There are a certain number of engineers who do not come under the terms of this Act so far as salaries, promotions, and pensions are concerned. Further amount required for surveys, examination of survey returns, printing of plans, &c., $320,000.

I would remind the right hon. gentleman that we have already voted $430,000, and now we are asked for $320,000 more. The vote last year was $360,000, so that the total increase this year is $390,000, or about 110 per cent more than was voted last year.

When the main estimates were prepared last fall, it was thought that $430,000 would be sudlcient, but the great influx of settlers from the United States and Europe, has made it imperative upon us to provide homesteads, and it was decided that this $320,000 should be inserted in the supplementary estimates, to sub-divide a sufficient number of townships to meet the wants of immigration. It is proposed to survey 500 new townships during the next fiscal year. At present, in south-eastern Manitoba there is one party under daily pay ; in the Yorkton district, one party under daily pay, renewing surveys ; between Lake Winnipeg and Manitoba one party under daily pay ; north of Battleford, two parties under daily pay ; in the Edmonton district, one party renewing surveys; in the Red Deer district, one party ; McLeod district, one party ; Rocky mountains, one party ; in British Columbia, two parties; and on unforeseen surveys, five parties. In the division of townships between Fort Perry and eastern Assiniboia and Edmonton, there are 60 contracts at $8,000 each, making $612,000 in all. The balance is for the following purposes :	Inspection of
surveys, $10,000; irrigation surveys, $20,000; Yukon surveys, $45,000; employees at Ottawa. $60,000; miscellaneous, $10,000. The total, $750,000. During the last twelve months 120,000 immigrants have gone in, and I think all will agree that this expenditure is absolutely Imperative.
How many immigrants did the right hon. gentleman say have gone in ?
Over 120,000 during the past fiscal year.
Are these sixty contracts let on schedule prices.
Yes.
Are they subdividing, or just blocking out townships ?
Subdividing. The pay varies according to the country, from $7 to $25.
You have raised the minimum pay $2.
I dare say, but it is a growing time.

Is that immigration which the right hon. gentleman speaks

of in the territories alone, or in Manitoba and the territories, or in the whole of Canada ?	_
That is for the whole of Canada.
Is there any estimate by the officers of the department as to how much of this immigration went to the territories ?
About and over 110,000 for Manitoba and the North-west Territories.	.
There is no estimate, I suppose, as between Manitoba and the North-west Territories 7
No.

I have a very distinct recollection of some animated discussions in this House with regard to the extravagance of using less than $300,000 for surveys. It was then said that lands were being surveyed that were not occupied and that it would be necessary later on to hunt uip the lines; yet now we are doing exactly the same thing. The salaries are apparently higher than those then paid and there are now sixteen government parties out and sixty contracts, seventy-six all told.
And imore are called for.
And more are called for; well, it is a very good thing the hon. gentleman is so well satisfied now; his friends were not so easily satisfied a few years ago.

My hon. friend would admit that we would be liable to be accused of being remiss in our duty if we did not provide facilities for incoming immigrants so that they may at once locate on homesteads. It may be that we have some divided lands that are not occupied, but I do not think we can very well cease surveying. All of the lots divided are not fit for settlement and the immigrants have a right to choose their land ; but on the whole we cannot go back on this work and I think my hon. friend will admit on reflection that it is a work of imperative necessity.

We have practically no information with regard to the salary or as to the value of the contracts. They are from $7 to $27. That is a sliding scale which is practically equivalent to no information at all and on which you cannot make any calculation. What do you give your surveyors now for a day's work 7
And found ?
Yes.

I noticed in a western paper the other day an allegation that the iron stakes which are used to mark the corners of the lots for settlement were being used for certain culinary purposes by
parties who are camping out; they were being used for the purpose of hanging camp kettles and things of that kind and, if as my hon. friend (Mr. Sproule) says, the stakes are sometimes pulled up, attention should be given to this by the department. I do not know' that the officers of the department have had information or not.

They have had information and have been obliged to give notice of prosecution if this is not stopped.
To provide for engraving, lithographing, printing, &e., to bring out maps of work already done, $10,500.

This item is explained by the words of the resolution; it is to cover the cost of engraving and lithographing maps, some of which are now in the hands of the engraver and others yet to be sent. These maps are chiefly of the Haliburton district, the country around Pembroke, Brockville, Sudbury, Copper Cliff, Boundary, the Klondike, and so on, different parts of the country of which maps are prepared.
Where are your maps made 7
They are lithographed here by the Federal Press Company.
Are any of these made in the United States 7
I am not aware of any and I do not think so, but I can inquire.
I heard a remark to that effect; I know the Minister of the Interior got out some of his maps in Chicago and it seems to me we should have brains enough to get them out here in Canada.
I think so, and this vote, so far as I know, .contemplates Canadian and not American work.
Would the right hon. Prime Minister be good enough to ascertain whether it will be so 7

I will.
To pay for metallurgical, petrographical and clerical assistance. (Salaries greater than $400 per annum may be paid from this vote, notwithstanding the Civil Service Act), $5,300.

This is to pay the salaries of the metallurgist and the as-sayer, Mr. Connor, and Mr. O. E. Leroy, the petographer. Both of these gentlemen do technical work. The balance of the vote is to meet sundry clerical work in connection with the department.
Where is the assayer employed ?
He is here in the Geological Survey.
Has he anything to do with the assay office ?
No.
Who is in charge of the assay office at Victoria ?
Mr. McCaffrey.

Yes. The next item is.$600, to pay the expenses of an inquiry into the cause of the disaster at Prank. Messrs. Connell and Brock made this inquiry.
Indians-Ontario and Quebec-to provide an amount for the repair of roads, $2,100.
Why are these roads being built ?

To explain that, I must explain also the next vote :
To provide an amount for squatters' improvements, Doncaster reserve, $11,325.
The township of Doncaster, in the county of Montcalm, district of Terrebonne, was set apart as an Indian reserve in 1853, for the Iroquois, of Oka and Caughnawaga. But, strange to say, the Indians never took possession of the reserve. They have never lived there, never made any settlement-have not even exercised the right of hunting there. As the country developed, squatters settled on the lands. These squatters applied for a title to the government at Quebec. When the matter was looked into the government at Quebec were obliged to inform these applicants that they could not give them a title, as the township was an Indian reserve. So, the squatters applied to the government at Ottawa for a title. We applied to the Indians at Caughnawaga and Oka to see if they would surrender their rights and take another reserve. But the Indians would not grant a transfer of the land. They insisted upon their rights, even to the extent of the dislodging of the whites. We made several applications to the Indians and the question was the subject of several conferences. We offered them land in some other parts of the country. Still, they insisted that the land belonged to them and would not surrender it, but called upon the Indian Department to dislodge the white settlers. We came to the conclusion that we were helpless in the matter, and would have to dislodge the whites. We could not do so without compensating the settlers. That is why we ask this appropriation of $11,325-to compensate the settlers for their improvements. This item with regard to the building of roads arises out of the same difficulty. The condition of things is particularly unfortunate, because there is a settlement all around the reserve as well as in the reserve itself. To keep faith with the Indians we must dislodge the white settlers in the township and to do that we must compensate the settlers, and also we must cut roads across Sir WILFRID LAURIER.
