I was giving this information to show that the department has taken every precaution, the first valuation having been confirmed with very slight variations by the second valuator. As I said a moment ago, there is nothing else that we can do but what we are doing. We

have to keep faith with the Indians. The land is theirs. On the other hand the settlers have gone* in on good faith, and, if they have to he removed, we have to ask for an appropriation to compensate them.
Could you charge anything to the Indian Department for the improvements made ?
I am afraid not. these Indians have but a very small fund.
The Prime Minister told us that the Oka Indians were interested in this land. Are these the Indians of Oka, whom the government have been removing to another locality for the last twenty years ?

A number of them were removed to a reserve on the Georgian bay, but they have all returned to Oka.
Contribution on behalf of the Rama Indians towards expenses on roads and bridges in the township of Rama, $2,000.
This is the old settled municipality-it has been settled for forty or fifty years. Does the government still keep up roads there ?

This is one of the cases where we have to keep up roads. It so happens that the reserve is not a compact block, but separate blocks, with Intervening blocks settled by white men. Where alternate parcels of land are occupied by white settlers and Indians, the municipality have no control over the reserve, and it is found impossible to maintain the regular system of roads. The same influence operates against a regular school system, as the children of the whites have to cross part of the reserve to reach the school, and this makes it difficult, practically impossible to maintain the schools on account of the inconvenience and extra expense.

I know the locality very well, and, no doubt, the difficulty with regard to the road is very considerable.
Nova Scotia-to provide an amount for the purchase of lands for reserves, $800.
This is for the purchase of 76 acres of wood land in Colchester county which the Indians require for cultivation and for fuel.

I think more attention might be given to some of these matters in Nova Scotia. I informed the department two years ago that certain lands reserved for Indians in the county of Halifax, and which were not used by the Indians, could be disposed of for a fair sum, but in the meantime they were being cut over by lumbermen and no precautions were being taken to prevent it. It seems to me that it would be better for the department to look after lands of that kind and see
that they are not used for lumbering operations by other people. If it is considered too expensive to provide safeguards for that purpose, it would be better to sell the lands. For example, you are buying land in Colchester county and paying a certain sum of money for it, and if I am correctly informed, there is land in the county of Halifax reserved for the Indians but which is not used by them, and the value of which is being materially depreciated. It is better to do something with it, exchange it, sell it, dispose of it, but do not let it be ruined.

The department would like to follow the suggestion of my hon. friend, but he knows that the first condition is to ob'tain a surrender of the land from the Indians. They are always averse to surrendering anything they have. I understand they are scattered all over the territory, and it is difficult to get them to agree. The question has been taken up several times by the department and they find that difficulty.
Is that the case with regard to the lands that are not occupied by the Indians, and are not actually in use 7
It applies to all reserves. The land cannot be disposed of without their consent.

It is an awkward state of affairs, because in the meantime the land is useless and is deteriorating.
Indians-New Brunswick-to provide an additional amount for salaries, $100.

This is to provide an increase of salary for Mr. W. B. Carter, who has charge of a large number of Indians. He is an active and competent officer.
To pay for damages by fire on the Indian reserve, Bdmundston, $100.

While clearing lands the Indians started fires on three occasions. in 1893. in 1894 and in 1895, which spread on to the property of Mr. Bernier, and destroyed his farm-house and fences.
Indians-Manitoba and North-west Territories-to provide an additional amount for implements, $1,500.
This is to purchase seed drills for the Touchwood Hills agency, and one threshing machine for the Duck Lake agency.

In the main estimates that vote was reduced by 84.288 and there was some jubilation in consequence. The amount of agricultural implements there was $7,540, instead of $12,237 the year before. Now you come again in the supplementary estimates and ask for an additional amount. This has occurred so many times that I think a little more common sense and business methods might be exercised in the

preparation of tlie main estimates. We have to take a vote over twice, both in the main estimates and the supplementary estimates, that ought to appear in the main estimates alone, and then we would know the full amount we are giving. It would save time and make the book-keeping much more simple.
I agree with what the hon. gentleman says, and I shall report it to the minister.

What I am complaining of is that we make the work double for ourselves. The main estimates ought to contain all that is required for the year. The main estimates this year must have been made up from the experience of last year, they were all submitted to council some time last winter. Surely it ought to be known from the experience of last year about what was required in every one of these lines? I could understand that accidentally something might he overlooked. But I find with regard to these items in Manitoba and the North-west Territories that the very same lines, agricultural implements, seed, livestock, clothing, cattle, surveys and schools, all appear in the main estimates.

The explanation is that the demands come early in the fall when the main estimates are prepared, but other demands come in afterwards. In the case of these agencies at Touchwood Hills and Duck Lake, I understand the applications came in too late for the main estimates. But we cannot leave them unprovided for, and hence the necessity for the supplementary estimates.
Additional amount tor triennial clothing,
This is provided for under treaty No. 8. This estimate came after the main estimates had been prepared. They were made after the inspector's return and could not have been provided for earlier.

You give the Indians a supply of clothing every three years. Can the minister say what Indians have been supplied each year, because they are not all supplied the same year ? Surely it Would have been as easy to take those who have not been supplied and send them in altogether?
The deputy commissioner informs me that it would be impossible to know the number of outfits that have to be provided until the inspector makes his report.
But he makes two reports.
The inspector leaves in the spring and does not return to civilization until late in the fall. That is the reason why we cannot obtain his report earlier.
To provide an additional amount for surveys, $2,000.
For surveys ?

Owing to the large amount of survey work being done iy Manitoba and the North-west Territories, tilt vote in the main estimates, $5,000, will be completely exhausted at the close of the year's operations. It is proposed to use the $2,000 to get the surveyors into the field early in the spring of 1904, so as to make the best possible use of their services.
Are not the reservations all surveyed before this ?

The reserve is set aside in a general way and we may not be required to make a survey for a long time until approaching settlement makes it necessary. That is the reason why surveys have been made from time to time.
To provide an additional amount for schools, $3,736.
Where are these schools that require an additional amount ?

To provide an amount to build a laundry at Rupert's Land Industrial School to replace the one destroyed by fire, one thousand dollars is required. To provide for the rebuilding of the laundry at the Battleford Industrial School lately destroyed by fire, $1,500 is required. To provide a grant towards the maintenance of a boarding school at Albany, on James' bay, $300. To provide for eight extra pupils at $75 at the Isle a la Crosse boarding school. $576 ; and to provide for five extra pupils at Thunder Child boarding school, $360, making altogether $3,736.
To provide an additional amount for general expenses (from which payments may be made to Dr. C. H. West, notwithstanding anything in the Civil Service Act), $2,200.
Why do you put it in that way ? Dr. West does not come under the Civil Service Act, does he ?

Dr. West is an inspector of the North-west Mounted Police in charge of the Athabasca district, and as such receives a salary of $1,000 per annum. It is proposed to continue his services ns medical attendant to the Indians of Treaty No. 8, and to pay him a salary of $1,200 therefor. Dr. West accompanies Inspector Conroy on his trips and gives medical relief to the Indians attending the treaty payment. Being a resident of the district he also attends all cases of sickness which are brought to his attention amongst those Indians.
Does that cover medicines as well as attendance ?

Yes, the $1,200 covers all services.

British Columbia-to provide an additional amount for salaries, $200.
Why is this necessary ?

Mr. Vowell was appointed Indian superintendent on the 4tli November, 1899, but before that date he had long been in the service of' the provincial government in the province of British Columbia, which renders his knowledge of the country especially valuable to this department. Since his appointment he has received no increase of salary and as there has been during the past few years a very considerable increase in the volume of work at the Victoria office it is thought that the proposed increase is merited.
To provide an additional amount for medical attendance and medicines, $9,000.

Medical attendance and medicines are provided for Indians who cannot afford to pay for it themselves. The physicians are either on salaries which represent a fair remuneration for their services and the medicine supplied, or when paid by accounts, they are allowed the lowest possible charges made to poor white patients. Medicines are supplied to medical missionaries to distribute them to Indians under their charge.
There has been $11,000 voted for medicines already. It seems a curious thing that you nearly double that amount by a supplementary estimate.
The sum which has been voted already is for medicines only.

No, it is for both. If my right hon. friend will turn to page 67 of the main estimates, he will see that, the item is :
Medical attendance and medicines, $11,000.
How many medical attendants have you employed, and what do you pay them ?

We have medical men in different parts of the province. British Columbia is a very large province and the Indian population of British Columbia is larger than that of any other province. In the Babine agency there is a medical attendant at Hazleton, Kishfyak and Hagincyet. In the Comox agency, Che-mainus, Nanaimo, Cowichan ; Fraser agency, Vancouver, Harrison, Hot Springs and New Westminster ; Kamloops and Okanagan, Fair View, Yale and Cariboo district, Ke-fowun and Cariboo district, Vernon and Cariboo district, Spallumcheen, Nicola, Kamloops, Dead men's Crest, Thompson and Shusliwap. , In the Kootenay : St. Mary's and Tobacco Plains ; on the west coast, Uculelet, Olayoquot ; on the north-west coast, Bella Bella, Port Simpson and vicinity, Port Essington, Williams Lake, Ques-nelle and Alexandria, Alkali Lake, Kenim, Soda Creek, Clinton.
What salaries do you pay ?
They vary ; $300, $500, $400, $700, $1,200 at Westminster and Vancouver.
Two months ago we voted $11,000 as sufficient for this purpose, and why should we require $9,000 more now ?
The estimates were prepared last fall on the reports in the department at that time, but new demands have been since made.

That does not seem to be a very satisfactory explanation. Unless there is some sudden outbreak of disease amongst Indians, surely the officers know the number of Indians in British Columbia, and they ought to be able to calculate within 20 per cent of what medical attendance they will require ; but this is double the vote of last year.
I am informed that the total vote last year was $20,000, the same as this year.
In the main estimates it says that last year's [DOT] vote was $11,000.
Perhaps it would be better to set out the total amount voted, but as a rule you will find that was only the amount voted in the main estimates last year.
Under what kind of a contract are these medical men working ?

There are 1,000 reserves in British Columbia, and as we have not a doctor for each reserve some of the doctors have to travel a good deal. They are appointed on a salary which is calculated upon the probable amount of work they will have to discharge.
I have heard it said out there that if a doctor wanted a holiday trip, lie goes round with the parties distributing the money and vaccinate some of these Indians, and makes a charge for it.
Oh, that was in the olden times.

I heard it last fall, and I do not think it is so very ancient.
To provide additional amount for schools,

This vote is distributed as follows :	Grant for rebuilding and equipping of the girls home, Met-lakahtla, destroyed by fire $3,200 ; to provide for an increase in the per capita grant to the Clayoquot school, $3,500 ; grant to-

wards the erection of boarding school at Ahonsaht, $1,500; to provide for repairs and addition to St. Mary's boarding school, $3,200.
Additional amount for steam launch, $2,500.

This agency includes 91 reserves, and to visit these the agent has to travel from 1,000 to 1,400 miles by canoe. If provided with a launch, the time at his disposal for visiting the Indians would be more than doubled, and his transportation expenses would not be materially increased.
Do they confine the mse of the launch to that purpose, or do they make a ferry boat of it ?

I do not know what he does with it, but I presume it remains idle when it is not being used for the purpose indicated. I do not think it would be used as a ferry boat.
Grant towards hospital at Hazelton, $1,000.

Two hundred and fifty thousand dollars of this is voted under circumstances with which the House is already familiar. The other $5,000 is required for registrars consequent upon the increased immigration.	,
What further facilities are to be provided ?
It simply provides for more clerical work and more assistance in the different registry offices.

It says :
Additional grant for schools, clerical assistance, printing, &c.
Why is the grant for schools made V
That item of $250,000 has been discussed.

This was discussed in connection with the Bill to make an advance to the North-west Territories. In connection with that Bill it was pointed out that we had increased the ordinary grant last year by $250,000 and this item is to make corresponding increase this year.
I do not think you gave any detailed information as to how this money was to be spent.
It is a general increase, equivalent to an increased subsidy to the North-west Territories.
